**TechCrunch** is an American global [online newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_newspaper "Online newspaper") focusing on topics regarding [high-tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_tech "High tech") and [startup companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company"). It was founded in June 2005 by Archimedes Ventures, led by partners [Michael Arrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Arrington "Michael Arrington") and [Keith Teare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Teare "Keith Teare").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-4) In 2010, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired the company for approximately $25 million. Following the 2015 [acquisition of AOL and Yahoo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Communications#Acquisition_of_AOL_and_Yahoo "Verizon Communications") by [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"), the site was owned by [Verizon Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Media "Verizon Media") from 2015 through 2021.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-:0-5)

In 2021, Verizon sold its media assets, including AOL, Yahoo!, and TechCrunch, to the private equity firm [Apollo Global Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Global_Management "Apollo Global Management"). Apollo integrated them into a new entity called [Yahoo! Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Inc._(2017%E2%80%93present) "Yahoo! Inc. (2017–present)")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-:0-5) In addition to its news reporting, TechCrunch is also known for its annual Disrupt conference, a technology event hosted in several cities across the United States, Europe, and China.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

TechCrunch was founded in June 2005 by Archimedes Ventures, led by partners [Michael Arrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Arrington "Michael Arrington") and [Keith Teare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Teare "Keith Teare"). In 2010, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired the company for approximately $25 million.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-6)As of 2013,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit) TechCrunch was available in English, Chinese (managed by Chinese tech news company TechNode),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-8) and Japanese.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-9) TechCrunch France was folded into the main TechCrunch.com site in October 2012.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-10) Boundless (formerly Verizon Media Japan), the Japanese subsidiary of the TechCrunch's parent company, closed TechCrunch Japan in May 2022 according to its "global strategy".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-12)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg/330px-Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg)

[Ethereum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethereum "Ethereum") founder [Vitalik Buterin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin "Vitalik Buterin") at the TechCrunch event in 2015

Following the [acquisition of AOL and Yahoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Communications#Acquisition_of_AOL_and_Yahoo "Verizon Communications") by [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"), TechCrunch was owned by [Verizon Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Media "Verizon Media") from 2015 through 2021.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-13) In August 2020, the COO of TechCrunch, Ned Desmond, stepped down after eight years in the company. He announced that he would join the [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital") firm [SOSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOSV "SOSV") in December 2020 as a senior operating partner.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-15) His former role at TechCrunch was replaced by Matthew Panzarino,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-16) former editor-in-chief, and Joey Hinson, director of business operations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-18)

In 2021, Verizon sold its media assets, including AOL, Yahoo, and TechCrunch, to the private equity firm [Apollo Global Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Global_Management "Apollo Global Management"), and Apollo integrated them into a new entity called [Yahoo! Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Inc._(2017%E2%80%93present) "Yahoo! Inc. (2017–present)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-19) TechCrunch's monthly visitors in September 2024 were 12.12 million, according to data from [SEMRush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semrush "Semrush").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-20) In March 2025, Yahoo! Inc. sold TechCrunch to private equity firm [Regent LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent_LP "Regent LP").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-21) A few months later _Sifted_ reported the website shut down its European operations, which was later denied by TechCrunch Chairman and Publisher Michael Reinstein.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-23)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Events")]

### TechCrunch Disrupt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: TechCrunch Disrupt")]

Starting in New York City in 2010, TechCrunch hosts an annual tech conference, TechCrunch Disrupt, in several cities in the United States and Europe. The event brings entrepreneurs, investors and tech enthusiasts together to watch startups pitch their ideas to a panel of judges, participate in networking events, listen to keynote speeches and panel discussions.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-25)

### Startup Battlefield

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Startup Battlefield")]

Startup Battlefield is a startup competition. Monetary awards are presented at the TechCrunch Disrupt conferences. Startup Battlefield has a reputation for launching some of the most successful companies in the tech industry. Notable startups that have been involved in the competition include [Dropbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropbox "Dropbox"), [Intuit Mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuit_Mint "Intuit Mint"), [Yammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yammer "Yammer"), Parallel Health, and [CrateDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CrateDB "CrateDB").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-28)

## Former features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Former features")]

### Crunchbase

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Crunchbase")]

From 2007 to 2015, TechCrunch operated [Crunchbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crunchbase "Crunchbase"), a website and [online encyclopedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_encyclopedia "Online encyclopedia") of information on startups, key people, funds, funding rounds, and events. In 2015, Crunchbase became a private entity and is no longer part of TechCrunch.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-30)

### Crunchies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Crunchies")]

From 2007 to 2017, TechCrunch sponsored the annual [Crunchies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crunchies "Crunchies") award ceremony to award startups, internet, and technology innovations.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-31) At the first award ceremony in 2007, [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") won the award for best [startup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company"). TechCrunch announced in 2017 that it would end the Crunchies.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-33)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In 2011, the site's editors and writers were criticized for possible [ethics violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics_violation "Ethics violation"). These included claims that Arrington's investments in certain firms that the site had covered created a [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-34) The controversy that ensued eventually led to Arrington's departure, and other writers, including [Paul Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Carr_(writer) "Paul Carr (writer)") and [Sarah Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Lacy "Sarah Lacy"), moved to another technology investment media company.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-36)

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2013, TechCrunch faced criticism for allowing a presentation of a mobile app called Titstare, created by two Australian developers. The app, which purportedly allowed users to share photos of men staring at women's breasts, was widely condemned as sexist and inappropriate. The incident drew negative media attention, including coverage from CNN and The Guardian, and prompted TechCrunch to issue a public apology and pledge stricter content review for future events.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-39)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

In 2014, TechCrunch Disrupt was featured in an arc of the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") series _[Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon\_Valley\_(TV\_series) "Silicon Valley (TV series)")_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-observer-40) The characters' startup "Pied Piper" participates in a startup battle at TechCrunch Disrupt.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-observer-40)

**TechCrunch** is an American global [online newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_newspaper "Online newspaper") focusing on topics regarding [high-tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_tech "High tech") and [startup companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company"). It was founded in June 2005 by Archimedes Ventures, led by partners [Michael Arrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Arrington "Michael Arrington") and [Keith Teare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Teare "Keith Teare").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-4) In 2010, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired the company for approximately $25 million. Following the 2015 [acquisition of AOL and Yahoo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Communications#Acquisition_of_AOL_and_Yahoo "Verizon Communications") by [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"), the site was owned by [Verizon Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Media "Verizon Media") from 2015 through 2021.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-:0-5)

In 2021, Verizon sold its media assets, including AOL, Yahoo!, and TechCrunch, to the private equity firm [Apollo Global Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Global_Management "Apollo Global Management"). Apollo integrated them into a new entity called [Yahoo! Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Inc._(2017%E2%80%93present) "Yahoo! Inc. (2017–present)")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-:0-5) In addition to its news reporting, TechCrunch is also known for its annual Disrupt conference, a technology event hosted in several cities across the United States, Europe, and China.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

TechCrunch was founded in June 2005 by Archimedes Ventures, led by partners [Michael Arrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Arrington "Michael Arrington") and [Keith Teare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Teare "Keith Teare"). In 2010, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired the company for approximately $25 million.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-6)As of 2013,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit) TechCrunch was available in English, Chinese (managed by Chinese tech news company TechNode),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-8) and Japanese.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-9) TechCrunch France was folded into the main TechCrunch.com site in October 2012.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-10) Boundless (formerly Verizon Media Japan), the Japanese subsidiary of the TechCrunch's parent company, closed TechCrunch Japan in May 2022 according to its "global strategy".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-12)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg/330px-Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vitalik_Buterin_TechCrunch_London_2015.jpg)

[Ethereum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethereum "Ethereum") founder [Vitalik Buterin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin "Vitalik Buterin") at the TechCrunch event in 2015

Following the [acquisition of AOL and Yahoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Communications#Acquisition_of_AOL_and_Yahoo "Verizon Communications") by [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"), TechCrunch was owned by [Verizon Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Media "Verizon Media") from 2015 through 2021.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-13) In August 2020, the COO of TechCrunch, Ned Desmond, stepped down after eight years in the company. He announced that he would join the [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital") firm [SOSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOSV "SOSV") in December 2020 as a senior operating partner.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-15) His former role at TechCrunch was replaced by Matthew Panzarino,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-16) former editor-in-chief, and Joey Hinson, director of business operations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-18)

In 2021, Verizon sold its media assets, including AOL, Yahoo, and TechCrunch, to the private equity firm [Apollo Global Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Global_Management "Apollo Global Management"), and Apollo integrated them into a new entity called [Yahoo! Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Inc._(2017%E2%80%93present) "Yahoo! Inc. (2017–present)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-19) TechCrunch's monthly visitors in September 2024 were 12.12 million, according to data from [SEMRush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semrush "Semrush").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-20) In March 2025, Yahoo! Inc. sold TechCrunch to private equity firm [Regent LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent_LP "Regent LP").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-21) A few months later _Sifted_ reported the website shut down its European operations, which was later denied by TechCrunch Chairman and Publisher Michael Reinstein.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-23)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Events")]

### TechCrunch Disrupt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: TechCrunch Disrupt")]

Starting in New York City in 2010, TechCrunch hosts an annual tech conference, TechCrunch Disrupt, in several cities in the United States and Europe. The event brings entrepreneurs, investors and tech enthusiasts together to watch startups pitch their ideas to a panel of judges, participate in networking events, listen to keynote speeches and panel discussions.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-25)

### Startup Battlefield

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Startup Battlefield")]

Startup Battlefield is a startup competition. Monetary awards are presented at the TechCrunch Disrupt conferences. Startup Battlefield has a reputation for launching some of the most successful companies in the tech industry. Notable startups that have been involved in the competition include [Dropbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropbox "Dropbox"), [Intuit Mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuit_Mint "Intuit Mint"), [Yammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yammer "Yammer"), Parallel Health, and [CrateDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CrateDB "CrateDB").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-28)

## Former features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Former features")]

### Crunchbase

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Crunchbase")]

From 2007 to 2015, TechCrunch operated [Crunchbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crunchbase "Crunchbase"), a website and [online encyclopedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_encyclopedia "Online encyclopedia") of information on startups, key people, funds, funding rounds, and events. In 2015, Crunchbase became a private entity and is no longer part of TechCrunch.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-30)

### Crunchies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Crunchies")]

From 2007 to 2017, TechCrunch sponsored the annual [Crunchies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crunchies "Crunchies") award ceremony to award startups, internet, and technology innovations.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-31) At the first award ceremony in 2007, [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") won the award for best [startup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company"). TechCrunch announced in 2017 that it would end the Crunchies.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-33)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In 2011, the site's editors and writers were criticized for possible [ethics violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics_violation "Ethics violation"). These included claims that Arrington's investments in certain firms that the site had covered created a [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-34) The controversy that ensued eventually led to Arrington's departure, and other writers, including [Paul Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Carr_(writer) "Paul Carr (writer)") and [Sarah Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Lacy "Sarah Lacy"), moved to another technology investment media company.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-36)

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2013, TechCrunch faced criticism for allowing a presentation of a mobile app called Titstare, created by two Australian developers. The app, which purportedly allowed users to share photos of men staring at women's breasts, was widely condemned as sexist and inappropriate. The incident drew negative media attention, including coverage from CNN and The Guardian, and prompted TechCrunch to issue a public apology and pledge stricter content review for future events.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-39)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=TechCrunch&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

In 2014, TechCrunch Disrupt was featured in an arc of the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") series _[Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon\_Valley\_(TV\_series) "Silicon Valley (TV series)")_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-observer-40) The characters' startup "Pied Piper" participates in a startup battle at TechCrunch Disrupt.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch#cite_note-observer-40)

**Suroosh Alvi** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): سروش علوی; born (1969-03-26)26 March 1969) is a Canadian journalist and filmmaker. He is a co-founder of [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), a digital media and broadcasting brand that at its height of operation was distributed in over 50 countries.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-Brownstein2000-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-2) Alvi is a travelled journalist and an executive producer of film, covering [youth culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_culture "Youth culture"), [news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News "News"), and [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") globally. He has hosted and produced documentaries investigating controversial issues, armed conflicts, movements, and subcultures, including [conflict minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_resource "Conflict resource") in the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"), the [takeover of Gaza by Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaza_(2007) "Battle of Gaza (2007)") in the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict"), and the rise of the [Pakistani Taliban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehrik-i-Taliban_Pakistan "Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan") and [global terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-4)

Originally covering Montreal's alternative culture scene, VICE has expanded to include a network of digital properties, including _VICE.com_, _TheCreatorsProject.com_, _Motherboard.tv_, and _Noisey.com_ as well as a cable and OTT network, a [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label"), an in-house [creative services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_services "Creative services") agency and a book publishing division. Today, VICE produces dozens of original video series, covering news, travel, music, arts, fashion and food, and has a network of correspondents and bureaus.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-5) As a journalist, Alvi has reported for [VICE on HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_on_HBO "Vice on HBO") and [VICE News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News "Vice News"), which together have received both [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") and [Peabody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Awards "Peabody Awards") awards.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-7)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Alvi was born in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Ontario, to [Pakistani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistanis "Pakistanis") parents,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-8) both of whom are academics; his mother is [Sajida S. Alvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajida_Alvi "Sajida Alvi"), whose focus is on [Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_studies "Islamic studies") and [Mughal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire") history[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9) and who is now [professor emerita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeritus "Emeritus") at [McGill University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-10) and his father is Sabir A. Alvi, professor emeritus in [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-11) Alvi studied [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") at McGill University.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-12)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Alvi launched [VICE magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)") with [Shane Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist) "Shane Smith (journalist)") and [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") in 1996, after the three men bought its precursor, _Voices of Montreal_, from Interimages Communications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-VICE_Knows_No_Boundaries-14)

In 2002, Alvi created [VICE Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine)#Record_label "Vice (magazine)"), the company's record label which has partnered with over 50 artists and sold more than 7 million albums worldwide. Its clients have included [Snoop Dogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snoop_Dogg "Snoop Dogg"), [Action Bronson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_Bronson "Action Bronson"), [Black Lips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Lips "Black Lips"), [Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_(band) "Justice (band)"), [Chromeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromeo "Chromeo"), [The Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Streets "The Streets"), [Bloc Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloc_Party "Bloc Party"), and [Death From Above 1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_from_Above_(band) "Death from Above (band)"). In 2011, Alvi launched a partnership between VICE Music and [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-16)

In 2006, as VICE was expanding from magazine publishing to video reporting, Alvi reported on a segment titled _Gun Markets of Pakistan_, in which he travelled to [Pakistan's northwestern tribal areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federally_Administered_Tribal_Areas "Federally Administered Tribal Areas") to cover illegal mass weapons production that was flourishing in the fallout of the [Soviet–Afghan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War "Soviet–Afghan War").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-17) Since then, he has covered stories from around the world, reporting on conflicts and unrest in the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan"), [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), and the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-21) He has also produced and hosted documentaries for VICE on HBO, VICE News and the [VICE Guide to Travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vice_Guide_to_Travel "The Vice Guide to Travel") series.

In 2007, Alvi co-directed and executive-produced _[Heavy Metal in Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy\_Metal\_in\_Baghdad "Heavy Metal in Baghdad")_ for [VICE Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), in which he travels to Iraq and follows the [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") band [Acrassicauda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrassicauda "Acrassicauda") during the fall of [Saddam Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein "Saddam Hussein") amidst the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"), beginning in 2003 after the [United States-led invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq"). The film was an official selection at the [2007 Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Toronto_International_Film_Festival "2007 Toronto International Film Festival") and the [2008 Berlin International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/58th_Berlin_International_Film_Festival "58th Berlin International Film Festival"), and was named Best Documentary at the [2008 Warsaw Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Film_Festival "Warsaw Film Festival").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-22)

In 2012, Alvi along with director [Andy Capper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Capper "Andy Capper") travelled VICE to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica"), where he produced the feature-length film, REINCARNATED, featuring Snoop Dogg. The film was accepted at the [2012 Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Toronto_International_Film_Festival "2012 Toronto International Film Festival") and had its U.S. premiere at the [2013 SXSW festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-23)

In 2014, Alvi served as a guest curator for the PHI Centre in Montreal and oversaw a month's worth of programming.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-VICE_Knows_No_Boundaries-14)

In 2017, VICE launched a multi-part series hosted by Alvi that examines "the origins and impact of the world's deadliest terrorist organizations: [al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda") in [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), [al-Shabaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Shabaab_(militant_group) "Al-Shabaab (militant group)") in [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia"), [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram") in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"), the [Tehrik-i-Taliban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehrik-i-Taliban_Pakistan "Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan") in Pakistan and the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") in Iraq."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-24)

In 2020, the _VICE Guide to Iran_, hosted by Alvi, was released shortly after the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Revolutionary_Guard_Corps "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps")' shoot-down of [Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_International_Airlines_Flight_752 "Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752") during an [Iran–United States standoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93United_States_relations_after_1979 "Iran–United States relations after 1979") as part of the [2019-2021 Persian Gulf crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93United_States_relations_during_the_first_Trump_administration#Escalation_in_tensions "Iran–United States relations during the first Trump administration"). In the feature-length documentary, Alvi interviews ordinary [Iranians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") about life under the [Islamic government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_Islamic_Republic_of_Iran "Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran") and covers the impact of [international sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_Iran "Sanctions against Iran") on the country after the [1979 Islamic Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"). He also interviews prominent Iranian political figures, including [Masoumeh Ebtekar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masoumeh_Ebtekar "Masoumeh Ebtekar") and [Hossein Sheikholeslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hossein_Sheikholeslam "Hossein Sheikholeslam"), who were among [the students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Student_Followers_of_the_Imam's_Line "Muslim Student Followers of the Imam's Line") involved in the [1979–1981 Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"). Sheikholeslam died in March 2020 after contracting [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), one month prior to the documentary's release.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-25)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Alvi resides in New York City. He is married,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-26) and has a son.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-27) He struggled with a [heroin addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid_use_disorder "Opioid use disorder") in his youth, and was in recovery following [rehabilitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_rehabilitation "Drug rehabilitation") when he co-founded [_VICE_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)") in 1994.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-28)

**Suroosh Alvi** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): سروش علوی; born (1969-03-26)26 March 1969) is a Canadian journalist and filmmaker. He is a co-founder of [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), a digital media and broadcasting brand that at its height of operation was distributed in over 50 countries.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-Brownstein2000-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-2) Alvi is a travelled journalist and an executive producer of film, covering [youth culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_culture "Youth culture"), [news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News "News"), and [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") globally. He has hosted and produced documentaries investigating controversial issues, armed conflicts, movements, and subcultures, including [conflict minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_resource "Conflict resource") in the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"), the [takeover of Gaza by Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaza_(2007) "Battle of Gaza (2007)") in the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict"), and the rise of the [Pakistani Taliban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehrik-i-Taliban_Pakistan "Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan") and [global terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-4)

Originally covering Montreal's alternative culture scene, VICE has expanded to include a network of digital properties, including _VICE.com_, _TheCreatorsProject.com_, _Motherboard.tv_, and _Noisey.com_ as well as a cable and OTT network, a [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label"), an in-house [creative services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_services "Creative services") agency and a book publishing division. Today, VICE produces dozens of original video series, covering news, travel, music, arts, fashion and food, and has a network of correspondents and bureaus.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-5) As a journalist, Alvi has reported for [VICE on HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_on_HBO "Vice on HBO") and [VICE News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News "Vice News"), which together have received both [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") and [Peabody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Awards "Peabody Awards") awards.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-7)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Alvi was born in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Ontario, to [Pakistani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistanis "Pakistanis") parents,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-8) both of whom are academics; his mother is [Sajida S. Alvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajida_Alvi "Sajida Alvi"), whose focus is on [Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_studies "Islamic studies") and [Mughal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire") history[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9) and who is now [professor emerita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeritus "Emeritus") at [McGill University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-10) and his father is Sabir A. Alvi, professor emeritus in [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-11) Alvi studied [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") at McGill University.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-12)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Alvi launched [VICE magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)") with [Shane Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist) "Shane Smith (journalist)") and [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") in 1996, after the three men bought its precursor, _Voices of Montreal_, from Interimages Communications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-VICE_Knows_No_Boundaries-14)

In 2002, Alvi created [VICE Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine)#Record_label "Vice (magazine)"), the company's record label which has partnered with over 50 artists and sold more than 7 million albums worldwide. Its clients have included [Snoop Dogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snoop_Dogg "Snoop Dogg"), [Action Bronson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_Bronson "Action Bronson"), [Black Lips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Lips "Black Lips"), [Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_(band) "Justice (band)"), [Chromeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromeo "Chromeo"), [The Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Streets "The Streets"), [Bloc Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloc_Party "Bloc Party"), and [Death From Above 1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_from_Above_(band) "Death from Above (band)"). In 2011, Alvi launched a partnership between VICE Music and [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-16)

In 2006, as VICE was expanding from magazine publishing to video reporting, Alvi reported on a segment titled _Gun Markets of Pakistan_, in which he travelled to [Pakistan's northwestern tribal areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federally_Administered_Tribal_Areas "Federally Administered Tribal Areas") to cover illegal mass weapons production that was flourishing in the fallout of the [Soviet–Afghan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War "Soviet–Afghan War").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-17) Since then, he has covered stories from around the world, reporting on conflicts and unrest in the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan"), [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), and the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-21) He has also produced and hosted documentaries for VICE on HBO, VICE News and the [VICE Guide to Travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vice_Guide_to_Travel "The Vice Guide to Travel") series.

In 2007, Alvi co-directed and executive-produced _[Heavy Metal in Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy\_Metal\_in\_Baghdad "Heavy Metal in Baghdad")_ for [VICE Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), in which he travels to Iraq and follows the [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") band [Acrassicauda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrassicauda "Acrassicauda") during the fall of [Saddam Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein "Saddam Hussein") amidst the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"), beginning in 2003 after the [United States-led invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq"). The film was an official selection at the [2007 Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Toronto_International_Film_Festival "2007 Toronto International Film Festival") and the [2008 Berlin International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/58th_Berlin_International_Film_Festival "58th Berlin International Film Festival"), and was named Best Documentary at the [2008 Warsaw Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Film_Festival "Warsaw Film Festival").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-22)

In 2012, Alvi along with director [Andy Capper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Capper "Andy Capper") travelled VICE to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica"), where he produced the feature-length film, REINCARNATED, featuring Snoop Dogg. The film was accepted at the [2012 Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Toronto_International_Film_Festival "2012 Toronto International Film Festival") and had its U.S. premiere at the [2013 SXSW festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-23)

In 2014, Alvi served as a guest curator for the PHI Centre in Montreal and oversaw a month's worth of programming.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-VICE_Knows_No_Boundaries-14)

In 2017, VICE launched a multi-part series hosted by Alvi that examines "the origins and impact of the world's deadliest terrorist organizations: [al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda") in [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), [al-Shabaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Shabaab_(militant_group) "Al-Shabaab (militant group)") in [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia"), [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram") in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"), the [Tehrik-i-Taliban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehrik-i-Taliban_Pakistan "Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan") in Pakistan and the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") in Iraq."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-24)

In 2020, the _VICE Guide to Iran_, hosted by Alvi, was released shortly after the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Revolutionary_Guard_Corps "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps")' shoot-down of [Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_International_Airlines_Flight_752 "Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752") during an [Iran–United States standoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93United_States_relations_after_1979 "Iran–United States relations after 1979") as part of the [2019-2021 Persian Gulf crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93United_States_relations_during_the_first_Trump_administration#Escalation_in_tensions "Iran–United States relations during the first Trump administration"). In the feature-length documentary, Alvi interviews ordinary [Iranians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") about life under the [Islamic government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_Islamic_Republic_of_Iran "Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran") and covers the impact of [international sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_Iran "Sanctions against Iran") on the country after the [1979 Islamic Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"). He also interviews prominent Iranian political figures, including [Masoumeh Ebtekar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masoumeh_Ebtekar "Masoumeh Ebtekar") and [Hossein Sheikholeslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hossein_Sheikholeslam "Hossein Sheikholeslam"), who were among [the students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Student_Followers_of_the_Imam's_Line "Muslim Student Followers of the Imam's Line") involved in the [1979–1981 Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"). Sheikholeslam died in March 2020 after contracting [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), one month prior to the documentary's release.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-25)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Suroosh_Alvi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Alvi resides in New York City. He is married,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-26) and has a son.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-9)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-27) He struggled with a [heroin addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid_use_disorder "Opioid use disorder") in his youth, and was in recovery following [rehabilitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_rehabilitation "Drug rehabilitation") when he co-founded [_VICE_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)") in 1994.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suroosh_Alvi#cite_note-28)

**Shane Smith** (born 28 September 1969) is a Canadian journalist and media executive.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-2) He is [executive chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_chairman "Executive chairman") of the international media company [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), operating an international network of digital channels, a television production studio, a record label, an in-house creative services agency, a book-publishing house, and a feature film division.

Smith was the CEO of Vice from its founding until March 2018.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Shane Smith was born in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa"), Ontario, on 28 September 1969.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-4) His parents were [Irish immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Canadians "Irish Canadians"); his father was a computer programmer, and his mother a paralegal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-7) He attended the [Lisgar Collegiate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisgar_Collegiate_Institute "Lisgar Collegiate Institute") and later graduated from [Carleton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleton_University "Carleton University") with a degree in English literature and [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)

Before Vice, Smith played in local punk bands, spent a brief time working in a bar in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), and travelled around [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe") before moving to [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Beginning at _Voice_, rebrand as _VICE_ and Szalwinski years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Beginning at Voice, rebrand as VICE and Szalwinski years")]

Smith joined Montreal's _Voice_ magazine (later _Voice of Montreal_) in 1994, where his childhood friend [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-13) already worked as assistant editor under Suroosh Alvi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-:4-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-16) The [counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture "Counterculture") magazine was subsidized by a [Quebec government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Quebec "Government of Quebec") program assisting welfare recipients in developing workplace skills. The three men renamed the magazine _Vice_ when they bought it from its publisher in 1996.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-18)

[Richard Szalwinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Szalwinski "Richard Szalwinski"), a Canadian software millionaire, acquired the magazine and relocated the operation to New York City in the late 1990s. Following the relocation, the magazine quickly developed a reputation for provocative and [politically incorrect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically_incorrect "Politically incorrect") content. Under Szalwinski's ownership, a few retail stores were opened in New York City and customers could purchase fashion items that were advertised in the magazine. However, due to the end of the [dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble"), the three founders eventually regained ownership of the _Vice_ brand, followed by closure of the stores.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Rob-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-21)

### Expansion of _VICE_, video content, brand deals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Expansion of VICE, video content, brand deals")]

Initially publishing print articles based on [offbeat alternative culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_culture "Alternative culture"), _VICE_ moved to creating news content and [social criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_criticism "Social criticism") on [multiple media platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimedia "Multimedia") in 2006. Smith remains an owner of the company, and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ has described Smith as "a cross between a punk rocker and [_Fortune 500_ Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) As a journalist Smith has travelled to locations including North Korea, Iran, Afghanistan, Libya, Kashmir, Liberia, Sudan, and Greenland, initially for the 2006 online TV series [_VICE Guide to Travel_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Guide_to_Travel "Vice Guide to Travel").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) Smith has continued as a correspondent for VICE, appearing in online content as well as the host of VICE's HBO show and VICE Special Reports.

In 2006, on the advice from the company's creative director [Spike Jonze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jonze "Spike Jonze"), VICE Media began expanding into [digital video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_video "Digital video"). This led to a massive expansion of VICE into new channels, including a partnership with [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") in 2010 for The Creators Project, as well as deals with partners like [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%93present) "Viacom (2005–present)"), [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-22) and HBO, led by Smith.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/ShaneSmith2017.jpg/250px-ShaneSmith2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ShaneSmith2017.jpg)

Shane Smith of [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media") during Mobile World Congress 2017

In April 2013, VICE started a new series with HBO, "VICE", in which Smith and other VICE correspondents cover news stories from around the globe. The show's second season won an Emmy for Outstanding Informational Series or Special.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-23) The show was picked up for two more 14-episode seasons by HBO in May 2014, which aired in 2015 and 2016.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-24) Based on the success of the weekly show, in 2015 [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") and VICE announced an expanded deal including a daily news show on [HBO Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Now "HBO Now") premiering in 2016, 32 VICE-produced specials over four years, and an expansion of the existing show from 14 to nearly 30 episodes per year. "VICE" started its 5th season of weekly broadcasts on HBO under the expanded episode deal on Friday, 24 February 2017.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-25)

In June 2014, it was reported that [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner") was negotiating to acquire a minority stake in VICE Media; among the company's plans were to give Vice Media control over the programming of HLN—a spin-off network of [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") which had recently struggled in its attempts to re-focus itself as a younger-skewing, social media-oriented news service. However, the deal fell through as the companies were unable to agree on a proper valuation, and VICE Media partnered with [A&E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A+E_Global_Media "A+E Global Media") for a 10% minority stake in VICE Media for $250 million, keeping VICE Media independent.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post-26) The following April, it was announced that A&E's channel H2 would be rebranded as VICELAND,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-THR-27) a lifestyle channel aimed at millennials. On 29 February 2016, VICE Media officially launched VICELAND with investment support by Disney and A&E.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-28)[Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney") has since increased their stake in VICE Media through A&E with two $200 million investments—the first in November 2015, followed by the second a week later in December 2015—for a roughly 10% stake to assist in funding programming and growth.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-New_York_Times_on_Disney_Investment-29)

In 2015, VICE partnered with several companies, including [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-30) Rogers Communications, [Live Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Nation "Live Nation"), [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") and [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), where VICE was a launch partner for Snapchat's "Discover" platform.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Hollywood_Reporter-31)

### _VICE_ peak years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: VICE peak years")]

Smith, in interviews, has mentioned the possibility of VICE [going public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPO "IPO"), saying in a 2015 interview: "There hasn't been a media company like this to go public in 15 years… the markets would love it", and he told CNBC in 2016 that "it's the best time in history to be a [content creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_creator "Content creator")."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-33)

In 2015, Smith accompanied US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") as part of the president's first historic visit to a federal prison,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post_2-34) interviewing Obama along with five non-violent drug offenders at [El Reno Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Correctional_Institution,_El_Reno "Federal Correctional Institution, El Reno"). He also conducted the first public interview with the [Eagles of Death Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagles_of_Death_Metal "Eagles of Death Metal") following the [2015 terrorist shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_2015_Paris_attacks "November 2015 Paris attacks") at their show at the [Bataclan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataclan_(theatre) "Bataclan (theatre)") in Paris that left 89 dead.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-VICE_Interview_With_Eagles_of_Death_Metal-35)

In 2015, _[Canadian Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Business "Canadian Business")_ placed him on "Canada's Richest People", claiming his net worth to be at $1.27 billion.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)

On 9 December 2016, HBO broadcast "Vice Special Report: A House Divided", which explores the political dysfunction in the United States during the Obama presidency. The 75-minute program features Smith interviewing influential US politicians including President Obama, former Speaker of the House [John Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner "John Boehner") and former House Majority Leader [Eric Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Cantor "Eric Cantor") to understand the development of excessive polarization and gridlock, culminating in the 2016 presidential election.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-37) It was nominated for an Emmy award.

On 22 June 2016, VICE Media unveiled a number of international deals that, by the end of 2017, would make its programs available in over 50 new territories, over 80 in total.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-39)

Smith stepped down as CEO of Vice Media in 2018, and was replaced by [A+E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks") CEO [Nancy Dubuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Dubuc "Nancy Dubuc"), while he took on the role Executive Chairman.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-40) After years of financial struggles and layoffs, Vice Media filed for bankruptcy and was sold in August 2023.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-41)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

From 2016, Smith resided in [Santa Monica, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California"), with his wife, Tamyka, and his three daughters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-42)

In 2021, his wife Tamyka filed for divorce.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-The-Blast-43)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)
