**Shane Smith** (born 28 September 1969) is a Canadian journalist and media executive.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-2) He is [executive chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_chairman "Executive chairman") of the international media company [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), operating an international network of digital channels, a television production studio, a record label, an in-house creative services agency, a book-publishing house, and a feature film division.

Smith was the CEO of Vice from its founding until March 2018.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Shane Smith was born in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa"), Ontario, on 28 September 1969.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-4) His parents were [Irish immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Canadians "Irish Canadians"); his father was a computer programmer, and his mother a paralegal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-7) He attended the [Lisgar Collegiate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisgar_Collegiate_Institute "Lisgar Collegiate Institute") and later graduated from [Carleton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleton_University "Carleton University") with a degree in English literature and [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)

Before Vice, Smith played in local punk bands, spent a brief time working in a bar in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), and travelled around [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe") before moving to [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Beginning at _Voice_, rebrand as _VICE_ and Szalwinski years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Beginning at Voice, rebrand as VICE and Szalwinski years")]

Smith joined Montreal's _Voice_ magazine (later _Voice of Montreal_) in 1994, where his childhood friend [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-13) already worked as assistant editor under Suroosh Alvi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-:4-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-16) The [counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture "Counterculture") magazine was subsidized by a [Quebec government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Quebec "Government of Quebec") program assisting welfare recipients in developing workplace skills. The three men renamed the magazine _Vice_ when they bought it from its publisher in 1996.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-18)

[Richard Szalwinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Szalwinski "Richard Szalwinski"), a Canadian software millionaire, acquired the magazine and relocated the operation to New York City in the late 1990s. Following the relocation, the magazine quickly developed a reputation for provocative and [politically incorrect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically_incorrect "Politically incorrect") content. Under Szalwinski's ownership, a few retail stores were opened in New York City and customers could purchase fashion items that were advertised in the magazine. However, due to the end of the [dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble"), the three founders eventually regained ownership of the _Vice_ brand, followed by closure of the stores.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Rob-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-21)

### Expansion of _VICE_, video content, brand deals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Expansion of VICE, video content, brand deals")]

Initially publishing print articles based on [offbeat alternative culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_culture "Alternative culture"), _VICE_ moved to creating news content and [social criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_criticism "Social criticism") on [multiple media platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimedia "Multimedia") in 2006. Smith remains an owner of the company, and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ has described Smith as "a cross between a punk rocker and [_Fortune 500_ Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) As a journalist Smith has travelled to locations including North Korea, Iran, Afghanistan, Libya, Kashmir, Liberia, Sudan, and Greenland, initially for the 2006 online TV series [_VICE Guide to Travel_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Guide_to_Travel "Vice Guide to Travel").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) Smith has continued as a correspondent for VICE, appearing in online content as well as the host of VICE's HBO show and VICE Special Reports.

In 2006, on the advice from the company's creative director [Spike Jonze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jonze "Spike Jonze"), VICE Media began expanding into [digital video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_video "Digital video"). This led to a massive expansion of VICE into new channels, including a partnership with [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") in 2010 for The Creators Project, as well as deals with partners like [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%93present) "Viacom (2005–present)"), [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-22) and HBO, led by Smith.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/ShaneSmith2017.jpg/250px-ShaneSmith2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ShaneSmith2017.jpg)

Shane Smith of [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media") during Mobile World Congress 2017

In April 2013, VICE started a new series with HBO, "VICE", in which Smith and other VICE correspondents cover news stories from around the globe. The show's second season won an Emmy for Outstanding Informational Series or Special.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-23) The show was picked up for two more 14-episode seasons by HBO in May 2014, which aired in 2015 and 2016.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-24) Based on the success of the weekly show, in 2015 [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") and VICE announced an expanded deal including a daily news show on [HBO Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Now "HBO Now") premiering in 2016, 32 VICE-produced specials over four years, and an expansion of the existing show from 14 to nearly 30 episodes per year. "VICE" started its 5th season of weekly broadcasts on HBO under the expanded episode deal on Friday, 24 February 2017.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-25)

In June 2014, it was reported that [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner") was negotiating to acquire a minority stake in VICE Media; among the company's plans were to give Vice Media control over the programming of HLN—a spin-off network of [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") which had recently struggled in its attempts to re-focus itself as a younger-skewing, social media-oriented news service. However, the deal fell through as the companies were unable to agree on a proper valuation, and VICE Media partnered with [A&E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A+E_Global_Media "A+E Global Media") for a 10% minority stake in VICE Media for $250 million, keeping VICE Media independent.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post-26) The following April, it was announced that A&E's channel H2 would be rebranded as VICELAND,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-THR-27) a lifestyle channel aimed at millennials. On 29 February 2016, VICE Media officially launched VICELAND with investment support by Disney and A&E.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-28)[Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney") has since increased their stake in VICE Media through A&E with two $200 million investments—the first in November 2015, followed by the second a week later in December 2015—for a roughly 10% stake to assist in funding programming and growth.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-New_York_Times_on_Disney_Investment-29)

In 2015, VICE partnered with several companies, including [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-30) Rogers Communications, [Live Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Nation "Live Nation"), [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") and [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), where VICE was a launch partner for Snapchat's "Discover" platform.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Hollywood_Reporter-31)

### _VICE_ peak years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: VICE peak years")]

Smith, in interviews, has mentioned the possibility of VICE [going public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPO "IPO"), saying in a 2015 interview: "There hasn't been a media company like this to go public in 15 years… the markets would love it", and he told CNBC in 2016 that "it's the best time in history to be a [content creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_creator "Content creator")."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-33)

In 2015, Smith accompanied US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") as part of the president's first historic visit to a federal prison,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post_2-34) interviewing Obama along with five non-violent drug offenders at [El Reno Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Correctional_Institution,_El_Reno "Federal Correctional Institution, El Reno"). He also conducted the first public interview with the [Eagles of Death Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagles_of_Death_Metal "Eagles of Death Metal") following the [2015 terrorist shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_2015_Paris_attacks "November 2015 Paris attacks") at their show at the [Bataclan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataclan_(theatre) "Bataclan (theatre)") in Paris that left 89 dead.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-VICE_Interview_With_Eagles_of_Death_Metal-35)

In 2015, _[Canadian Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Business "Canadian Business")_ placed him on "Canada's Richest People", claiming his net worth to be at $1.27 billion.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)

On 9 December 2016, HBO broadcast "Vice Special Report: A House Divided", which explores the political dysfunction in the United States during the Obama presidency. The 75-minute program features Smith interviewing influential US politicians including President Obama, former Speaker of the House [John Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner "John Boehner") and former House Majority Leader [Eric Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Cantor "Eric Cantor") to understand the development of excessive polarization and gridlock, culminating in the 2016 presidential election.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-37) It was nominated for an Emmy award.

On 22 June 2016, VICE Media unveiled a number of international deals that, by the end of 2017, would make its programs available in over 50 new territories, over 80 in total.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-39)

Smith stepped down as CEO of Vice Media in 2018, and was replaced by [A+E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks") CEO [Nancy Dubuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Dubuc "Nancy Dubuc"), while he took on the role Executive Chairman.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-40) After years of financial struggles and layoffs, Vice Media filed for bankruptcy and was sold in August 2023.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-41)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

From 2016, Smith resided in [Santa Monica, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California"), with his wife, Tamyka, and his three daughters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-42)

In 2021, his wife Tamyka filed for divorce.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-The-Blast-43)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Awards")]

Smith's work on VICE's HBO show won him an [Emmy award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_award "Emmy award") in 2014, as well as a number of environmental awards for his work covering [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming") in Greenland, Antarctica and beyond. He has also been honoured with a Frank Stanton Award for Excellence in Communication,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-45) an LA Press Club Award,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-46) and two [Peabody awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_award "Peabody award")[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-47) for serving as executive producer of _VICE News_' documentaries "The Islamic State" and "Last Chance High".

**Shane Smith** (born 28 September 1969) is a Canadian journalist and media executive.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-2) He is [executive chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_chairman "Executive chairman") of the international media company [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media"), operating an international network of digital channels, a television production studio, a record label, an in-house creative services agency, a book-publishing house, and a feature film division.

Smith was the CEO of Vice from its founding until March 2018.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Shane Smith was born in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa"), Ontario, on 28 September 1969.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-4) His parents were [Irish immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Canadians "Irish Canadians"); his father was a computer programmer, and his mother a paralegal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-7) He attended the [Lisgar Collegiate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisgar_Collegiate_Institute "Lisgar Collegiate Institute") and later graduated from [Carleton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleton_University "Carleton University") with a degree in English literature and [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)

Before Vice, Smith played in local punk bands, spent a brief time working in a bar in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), and travelled around [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe") before moving to [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Beginning at _Voice_, rebrand as _VICE_ and Szalwinski years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Beginning at Voice, rebrand as VICE and Szalwinski years")]

Smith joined Montreal's _Voice_ magazine (later _Voice of Montreal_) in 1994, where his childhood friend [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-13) already worked as assistant editor under Suroosh Alvi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-:4-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-16) The [counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture "Counterculture") magazine was subsidized by a [Quebec government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Quebec "Government of Quebec") program assisting welfare recipients in developing workplace skills. The three men renamed the magazine _Vice_ when they bought it from its publisher in 1996.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-18)

[Richard Szalwinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Szalwinski "Richard Szalwinski"), a Canadian software millionaire, acquired the magazine and relocated the operation to New York City in the late 1990s. Following the relocation, the magazine quickly developed a reputation for provocative and [politically incorrect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically_incorrect "Politically incorrect") content. Under Szalwinski's ownership, a few retail stores were opened in New York City and customers could purchase fashion items that were advertised in the magazine. However, due to the end of the [dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble"), the three founders eventually regained ownership of the _Vice_ brand, followed by closure of the stores.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Rob-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-21)

### Expansion of _VICE_, video content, brand deals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Expansion of VICE, video content, brand deals")]

Initially publishing print articles based on [offbeat alternative culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_culture "Alternative culture"), _VICE_ moved to creating news content and [social criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_criticism "Social criticism") on [multiple media platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimedia "Multimedia") in 2006. Smith remains an owner of the company, and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ has described Smith as "a cross between a punk rocker and [_Fortune 500_ Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) As a journalist Smith has travelled to locations including North Korea, Iran, Afghanistan, Libya, Kashmir, Liberia, Sudan, and Greenland, initially for the 2006 online TV series [_VICE Guide to Travel_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Guide_to_Travel "Vice Guide to Travel").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-nyt-1) Smith has continued as a correspondent for VICE, appearing in online content as well as the host of VICE's HBO show and VICE Special Reports.

In 2006, on the advice from the company's creative director [Spike Jonze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jonze "Spike Jonze"), VICE Media began expanding into [digital video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_video "Digital video"). This led to a massive expansion of VICE into new channels, including a partnership with [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") in 2010 for The Creators Project, as well as deals with partners like [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%93present) "Viacom (2005–present)"), [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-22) and HBO, led by Smith.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/ShaneSmith2017.jpg/250px-ShaneSmith2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ShaneSmith2017.jpg)

Shane Smith of [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media "Vice Media") during Mobile World Congress 2017

In April 2013, VICE started a new series with HBO, "VICE", in which Smith and other VICE correspondents cover news stories from around the globe. The show's second season won an Emmy for Outstanding Informational Series or Special.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-23) The show was picked up for two more 14-episode seasons by HBO in May 2014, which aired in 2015 and 2016.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-24) Based on the success of the weekly show, in 2015 [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") and VICE announced an expanded deal including a daily news show on [HBO Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Now "HBO Now") premiering in 2016, 32 VICE-produced specials over four years, and an expansion of the existing show from 14 to nearly 30 episodes per year. "VICE" started its 5th season of weekly broadcasts on HBO under the expanded episode deal on Friday, 24 February 2017.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-25)

In June 2014, it was reported that [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner") was negotiating to acquire a minority stake in VICE Media; among the company's plans were to give Vice Media control over the programming of HLN—a spin-off network of [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") which had recently struggled in its attempts to re-focus itself as a younger-skewing, social media-oriented news service. However, the deal fell through as the companies were unable to agree on a proper valuation, and VICE Media partnered with [A&E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A+E_Global_Media "A+E Global Media") for a 10% minority stake in VICE Media for $250 million, keeping VICE Media independent.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post-26) The following April, it was announced that A&E's channel H2 would be rebranded as VICELAND,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-THR-27) a lifestyle channel aimed at millennials. On 29 February 2016, VICE Media officially launched VICELAND with investment support by Disney and A&E.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-28)[Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney") has since increased their stake in VICE Media through A&E with two $200 million investments—the first in November 2015, followed by the second a week later in December 2015—for a roughly 10% stake to assist in funding programming and growth.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-New_York_Times_on_Disney_Investment-29)

In 2015, VICE partnered with several companies, including [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-30) Rogers Communications, [Live Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Nation "Live Nation"), [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") and [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), where VICE was a launch partner for Snapchat's "Discover" platform.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Hollywood_Reporter-31)

### _VICE_ peak years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: VICE peak years")]

Smith, in interviews, has mentioned the possibility of VICE [going public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPO "IPO"), saying in a 2015 interview: "There hasn't been a media company like this to go public in 15 years… the markets would love it", and he told CNBC in 2016 that "it's the best time in history to be a [content creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_creator "Content creator")."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-33)

In 2015, Smith accompanied US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") as part of the president's first historic visit to a federal prison,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Huffington_Post_2-34) interviewing Obama along with five non-violent drug offenders at [El Reno Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Correctional_Institution,_El_Reno "Federal Correctional Institution, El Reno"). He also conducted the first public interview with the [Eagles of Death Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagles_of_Death_Metal "Eagles of Death Metal") following the [2015 terrorist shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_2015_Paris_attacks "November 2015 Paris attacks") at their show at the [Bataclan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataclan_(theatre) "Bataclan (theatre)") in Paris that left 89 dead.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-VICE_Interview_With_Eagles_of_Death_Metal-35)

In 2015, _[Canadian Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Business "Canadian Business")_ placed him on "Canada's Richest People", claiming his net worth to be at $1.27 billion.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-Canadian_Business-32)

On 9 December 2016, HBO broadcast "Vice Special Report: A House Divided", which explores the political dysfunction in the United States during the Obama presidency. The 75-minute program features Smith interviewing influential US politicians including President Obama, former Speaker of the House [John Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner "John Boehner") and former House Majority Leader [Eric Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Cantor "Eric Cantor") to understand the development of excessive polarization and gridlock, culminating in the 2016 presidential election.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-37) It was nominated for an Emmy award.

On 22 June 2016, VICE Media unveiled a number of international deals that, by the end of 2017, would make its programs available in over 50 new territories, over 80 in total.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-39)

Smith stepped down as CEO of Vice Media in 2018, and was replaced by [A+E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks") CEO [Nancy Dubuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Dubuc "Nancy Dubuc"), while he took on the role Executive Chairman.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-40) After years of financial struggles and layoffs, Vice Media filed for bankruptcy and was sold in August 2023.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-41)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

From 2016, Smith resided in [Santa Monica, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California"), with his wife, Tamyka, and his three daughters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-WSJ-Goldman-12)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-42)

In 2021, his wife Tamyka filed for divorce.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-The-Blast-43)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-vf2021-9)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shane_Smith_(journalist)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Awards")]

Smith's work on VICE's HBO show won him an [Emmy award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_award "Emmy award") in 2014, as well as a number of environmental awards for his work covering [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming") in Greenland, Antarctica and beyond. He has also been honoured with a Frank Stanton Award for Excellence in Communication,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-45) an LA Press Club Award,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-46) and two [Peabody awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_award "Peabody award")[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist)#cite_note-47) for serving as executive producer of _VICE News_' documentaries "The Islamic State" and "Last Chance High".

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers

**Jonah H. Peretti**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-1) (born January 1, 1974) is an American [internet entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_entrepreneur "Internet entrepreneur"). He is a co-founder and former [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEO "CEO") of [BuzzFeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed "BuzzFeed"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-2) a co-founder of _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_, and a developer of [reblogging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reblogging "Reblogging") under the project "Reblog".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-forbes-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-6)

## Education and early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education and early career")]

Peretti was born in California, and raised in [Oakland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-7) His father, a [criminal defense lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_defense_lawyer "Criminal defense lawyer") and [painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painter "Painter"), is of [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians") and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people") descent and his mother (_née_ Cherkin), a [schoolteacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolteacher "Schoolteacher"), is [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"). His stepmother was [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-9) He attended [The College Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_College_Preparatory_School "The College Preparatory School") in Oakland, followed by the [University of California, Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Cruz "University of California, Santa Cruz"), where he graduated with a degree in [environmental studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies") in 1996.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4) He taught [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science") classes at [Isidore Newman School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidore_Newman_School "Isidore Newman School") in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"), in the mid-1990s.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-10) He received a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") from the [MIT Media Lab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Media_Lab "MIT Media Lab") in 2001.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11)

While at MIT, his email exchange[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-email_exchange-12) with [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") over a request to print "[sweatshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweatshop "Sweatshop")" on custom order shoes went viral.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Fortune-13)

After graduating from the University of California, Santa Cruz in 1996, Peretti published an article titled _"Capitalism and Schizophrenia"_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-15) in _Negations,_ a Texas-based[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-16) journal of critical theory.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-17) The paper compares the text _Postmodernism and Consumer Society_, by [Fredric Jameson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredric_Jameson "Fredric Jameson"), with [Deleuze and Guattari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deleuze_and_Guattari "Deleuze and Guattari")'s [Anti-Oedipus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Oedipus "Anti-Oedipus") (along with discussing works by [Jacques Lacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Lacan "Jacques Lacan"), [Roland Barthes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Barthes "Roland Barthes") and [Jean Laplanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Laplanche "Jean Laplanche")) to demonstrate the "psychological link between one-dimensionality and advertising".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-18) It explains Peretti's ideas around viral marketing,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Vox-14)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-19) and offers examples of how anti-capitalist critique can be easily integrated into capitalism.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-20)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Peretti co-founded _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ along with [Kenneth Lerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Lerer "Kenneth Lerer"), [Andrew Breitbart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart "Andrew Breitbart") and [Arianna Huffington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington "Arianna Huffington") in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Buzzfeed-21) He left _The Huffington Post_ in 2011 after it was bought by [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") for $315 million.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Wired-22)

Peretti founded the "Internet popularity contest" site [BuzzFeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed "BuzzFeed") in November 2006.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Poynter-23) After leaving _The Huffington Post_, Peretti began working at BuzzFeed full-time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11) While originally known for its mix of [internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme "Internet meme") and [listicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listicle "Listicle"), the site was the first to break the news that [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") would endorse [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") in the [2012 Republican primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Republican_primary "2012 Republican primary").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11) The site continued to grow afterward, raising over $35 million in funding from investors the next year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYMag-24) In August 2014, the site raised another $50 million from the [venture capital firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital_firm "Venture capital firm")[Andreessen Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz"), more than doubling its previous [rounds of funding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_of_funding "Round of funding").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-CNN-25) The site was valued at $850 million by Andreessen Horowitz.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-CNN-25)

In 2019, Peretti announced that BuzzFeed would be cutting its overall workforce by 15 percent. Peretti said he wanted to reduce costs without resorting to additional fundraising.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-27) Its remaining workforce then officially unionized, their first successful fight being over laid-off staffers getting their earned paid time off.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-28)

In 2021 at a virtual company meeting, Peretti, as BuzzFeed's chief executive, fired 47 employees at _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ in a controversial manner, sending a virtual meeting password "spr!ngisH3r3" to laid-off employees. The HuffPost Union, which is affiliated with the Writers Guild of America East, said in a statement that the layoffs had affected 33 of its members, nearly a third of the local union.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-29)

In 2022, shareholders urged Peretti to shut down BuzzFeed News; two anonymous sources told CNBC that BuzzFeed News lost about $10 million annually.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-30) On April 20, 2023, BuzzFeed under Peretti laid off 15% of its staff and shut down the [BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed_News "BuzzFeed News") division. In an email to staff on April 20, Peretti stated that the company overinvested in BuzzFeed News "because I love their work and mission so much".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-31)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

He is the elder brother of [comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedian "Comedian"), actress and writer [Chelsea Peretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Peretti "Chelsea Peretti").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-MMag-32) He is married to blogger Andrea Harner, with whom he has twin sons.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-MMag-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-34)

**Jonah H. Peretti**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-1) (born January 1, 1974) is an American [internet entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_entrepreneur "Internet entrepreneur"). He is a co-founder and former [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEO "CEO") of [BuzzFeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed "BuzzFeed"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-2) a co-founder of _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_, and a developer of [reblogging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reblogging "Reblogging") under the project "Reblog".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-forbes-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-6)

## Education and early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education and early career")]

Peretti was born in California, and raised in [Oakland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-7) His father, a [criminal defense lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_defense_lawyer "Criminal defense lawyer") and [painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painter "Painter"), is of [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians") and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people") descent and his mother (_née_ Cherkin), a [schoolteacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolteacher "Schoolteacher"), is [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"). His stepmother was [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-9) He attended [The College Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_College_Preparatory_School "The College Preparatory School") in Oakland, followed by the [University of California, Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Cruz "University of California, Santa Cruz"), where he graduated with a degree in [environmental studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies") in 1996.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4) He taught [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science") classes at [Isidore Newman School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidore_Newman_School "Isidore Newman School") in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"), in the mid-1990s.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-10) He received a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") from the [MIT Media Lab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Media_Lab "MIT Media Lab") in 2001.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11)

While at MIT, his email exchange[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-email_exchange-12) with [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") over a request to print "[sweatshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweatshop "Sweatshop")" on custom order shoes went viral.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Fortune-13)

After graduating from the University of California, Santa Cruz in 1996, Peretti published an article titled _"Capitalism and Schizophrenia"_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-15) in _Negations,_ a Texas-based[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-16) journal of critical theory.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-17) The paper compares the text _Postmodernism and Consumer Society_, by [Fredric Jameson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredric_Jameson "Fredric Jameson"), with [Deleuze and Guattari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deleuze_and_Guattari "Deleuze and Guattari")'s [Anti-Oedipus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Oedipus "Anti-Oedipus") (along with discussing works by [Jacques Lacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Lacan "Jacques Lacan"), [Roland Barthes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Barthes "Roland Barthes") and [Jean Laplanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Laplanche "Jean Laplanche")) to demonstrate the "psychological link between one-dimensionality and advertising".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-18) It explains Peretti's ideas around viral marketing,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Vox-14)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-19) and offers examples of how anti-capitalist critique can be easily integrated into capitalism.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-20)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Peretti co-founded _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ along with [Kenneth Lerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Lerer "Kenneth Lerer"), [Andrew Breitbart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart "Andrew Breitbart") and [Arianna Huffington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington "Arianna Huffington") in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-independent-4)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Buzzfeed-21) He left _The Huffington Post_ in 2011 after it was bought by [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") for $315 million.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Wired-22)

Peretti founded the "Internet popularity contest" site [BuzzFeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed "BuzzFeed") in November 2006.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-Poynter-23) After leaving _The Huffington Post_, Peretti began working at BuzzFeed full-time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11) While originally known for its mix of [internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme "Internet meme") and [listicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listicle "Listicle"), the site was the first to break the news that [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") would endorse [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") in the [2012 Republican primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Republican_primary "2012 Republican primary").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYT-11) The site continued to grow afterward, raising over $35 million in funding from investors the next year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-NYMag-24) In August 2014, the site raised another $50 million from the [venture capital firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital_firm "Venture capital firm")[Andreessen Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz"), more than doubling its previous [rounds of funding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_of_funding "Round of funding").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-CNN-25) The site was valued at $850 million by Andreessen Horowitz.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-CNN-25)

In 2019, Peretti announced that BuzzFeed would be cutting its overall workforce by 15 percent. Peretti said he wanted to reduce costs without resorting to additional fundraising.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-27) Its remaining workforce then officially unionized, their first successful fight being over laid-off staffers getting their earned paid time off.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-28)

In 2021 at a virtual company meeting, Peretti, as BuzzFeed's chief executive, fired 47 employees at _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ in a controversial manner, sending a virtual meeting password "spr!ngisH3r3" to laid-off employees. The HuffPost Union, which is affiliated with the Writers Guild of America East, said in a statement that the layoffs had affected 33 of its members, nearly a third of the local union.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-29)

In 2022, shareholders urged Peretti to shut down BuzzFeed News; two anonymous sources told CNBC that BuzzFeed News lost about $10 million annually.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-30) On April 20, 2023, BuzzFeed under Peretti laid off 15% of its staff and shut down the [BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed_News "BuzzFeed News") division. In an email to staff on April 20, Peretti stated that the company overinvested in BuzzFeed News "because I love their work and mission so much".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-31)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jonah_Peretti&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

He is the elder brother of [comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedian "Comedian"), actress and writer [Chelsea Peretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Peretti "Chelsea Peretti").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-MMag-32) He is married to blogger Andrea Harner, with whom he has twin sons.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-MMag-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti#cite_note-34)

**BuzzFeed, Inc.** is an American [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet")[media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_media "Mass media"), news, and entertainment company with a focus on [digital media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media "Digital media"). Based in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-2) BuzzFeed was founded in 2006 by Jonah Peretti and [John S. Johnson III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Seward_Johnson_III "John Seward Johnson III") to focus on tracking viral content.

Originally known for online quizzes, "[listicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listicle "Listicle")," and pop culture articles, the company has grown into a global media and technology company across several subsidiary publications, providing coverage on a variety of topics including politics, [DIY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DIY "DIY"), animals, and business.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-LaFrance&Meyer-Atlantic-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-4) BuzzFeed generates revenue through [native advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising "Native advertising"), a strategy that helps increase the likelihood of viewers reading through the content of advertisements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-5)

In late 2011, BuzzFeed hired [Ben Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Smith_(journalist) "Ben Smith (journalist)") of _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ as editor-in-chief, to expand the site into [long-form journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-form_journalism "Long-form journalism") and reportage under the _[BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed\_News "BuzzFeed News")_ banner.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-6) After years of investment in investigative journalism, by 2021 BuzzFeed News had won the [National Magazine Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Magazine_Awards "National Magazine Awards"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:1-7) the [George Polk Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Polk_Awards "George Polk Awards"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:2-8) and the [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Robertson-9) and was nominated for the [Michael Kelly Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Kelly_Award "Michael Kelly Award").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:1-7)_BuzzFeed News_ later moved to its own domain rather than existing as a section of the main BuzzFeed website.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-10) On April 20, 2023, Peretti announced that BuzzFeed would be shuttering _BuzzFeed News_ and focusing its news efforts into _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_, laying off about 180 workers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-11)

After initially going public via a [special-purpose acquisition company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special-purpose_acquisition_company "Special-purpose acquisition company") in 2021 with a valuation of $1.5 billion, its stock price and valuation sharply declined to only being worth $37 million by 2024, and the company entered financial difficulties. In 2026 it was announced that the company was set to be purchased by [Byron Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Allen "Byron Allen")'s family office for $120 million. The sale was completed on May 27, 2026.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-12)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Jonah-peretti.jpg/250px-Jonah-peretti.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jonah-peretti.jpg)

Jonah Peretti founded BuzzFeed in November 2006.

Prior to establishing BuzzFeed, Peretti was director of [research and development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_development "Research and development") for the OpenLab at [Eyebeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyebeam_(organization) "Eyebeam (organization)"), John Johnson's New York City-based art and technology nonprofit organization, where he experimented with other viral media.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-14)

In 2006, while working at the _Huffington Post_, Peretti started BuzzFeed (originally called BuzzFeed Laboratories)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-15) as a side project, in partnership with his former supervisor Johnson. In the beginning, BuzzFeed employed no writers or editors, just an "algorithm to cull stories from around the web that were showing stirrings of virality."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-16) The site initially launched an instant messaging client, BuzzBot, which sent users a link to popular content. The messages were sent based on algorithms which examined the links that were being quickly disseminated, scouring through the feeds of hundreds of blogs that were aggregating them.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Later, the site began spotlighting the most popular links that BuzzBot found. Peretti hired curators to help describe the content that was popular around the web.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-insidebuzzfeed-17) In 2011, Peretti hired _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")'_ s Ben Smith, who earlier had achieved much attention as a political blogger, to assemble a news operation in addition to the many aggregated "listicles".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-18)

In 2016, BuzzFeed formally separated its news and entertainment content into _[BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed\_News "BuzzFeed News")_ and the newly formed BuzzFeed Entertainment Group, which also includes BuzzFeed Motion Pictures.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-20)As of 2016[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit), BuzzFeed had correspondents from 12 countries,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Robischon-FC-Quest-21) and foreign editions in Australia, Brazil, France, Germany, India, Japan, Mexico, Spain, and the United Kingdom.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-22)By the end of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit), BuzzFeed employed around 1,700 employees worldwide, although it announced plans in November of that year to lay off around 100 employees in the US, 45 in the UK,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-AP-layoff-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-25) and 100 in France in June 2018.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-26)

On January 23, 2019, BuzzFeed notified all employees via memo that there would be an upcoming 15% reduction in workforce affecting the international, web content, and news divisions of the company. The layoffs would affect approximately 200 employees.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-27) In 2020, BuzzFeed signed a deal with [Universal Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Television "Universal Television") to produce content based on its stories.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-28)

Three top _[BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed\_News "BuzzFeed News")_ editors in March 2022 announced that they would be resigning and the newsroom would face voluntary layoffs or job cuts.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-29) The cuts came after BuzzFeed investors encouraged Peretti to shut down all of _[BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed\_News "BuzzFeed News")_, but he refused, CNBC reported.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-30) In January 2023, Peretti announced that BuzzFeed would be making a "hard pivot" to AI generated content such as custom quizzes. In May 2023, Peretti announced that AI content would "replace the majority of static content" on the BuzzFeed website.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:4-31)

In March 2026, BuzzFeed revealed that it is still burdened by legacy commitments and it has engaged in "strategic conversations" about relieving its liquidity issues.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-auto-32)

In May 2026, it was announced that businessman [Byron Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Allen "Byron Allen") had agreed to buy the company for $120 million. As part of the acquisition, Peretti would step down as CEO and by replaced by Allen, though Peretti would stay on as head of BuzzFeed AI.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-34)

Following the acquisition, BuzzFeed began a restructuring under Allen with the intention of the company competing with [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"), 3 divisions were created with artificial intelligence assets being placed under BuzzFeed AI, shows and studio assets (such as Animation Lab) being placed under BuzzFeed Studios and food products being placed under Tasty.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-36)

### Funding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Funding")]

![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg/60px-Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This section needs to be **updated**. The reason given is: **advertising information from 2012 and expansion plans from 2015**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information._(March 2019)_

Despite reaching annual revenues in the hundreds of million of dollars at its peak, BuzzFeed has been consistently loss-making since its inception.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:5-37)

BuzzFeed raised $3.5 million in 2008 through Hearst Ventures and [SoftBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Ad_Age_Digital_A-List:_Buzzfeed-38) In 2011, BuzzFeed ran more than 100 social media campaigns, resulting in their revenue tripling compared to 2010.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Ad_Age_Digital_A-List:_Buzzfeed-38) In January 2012, BuzzFeed announced that it had earned $15.5 million in funding from [New Enterprise Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Enterprise_Associates "New Enterprise Associates"), Lerer Ventures, Hearst Interactive Media, SoftBank, and RRE Capital to expand the site's content.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-39) Later, in October 2012, BuzzFeed ran sponsored content for the Obama administration leading to an increase in ad revenue.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-40) By January 2013, BuzzFeed announced that New Enterprise Associates had raised $19.3 million.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-41) The company was reported to be profitable in 2013.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-42)

In 2014, it was reported that BuzzFeed had passed $100 million in revenue.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Reuters_2016-44) In August 2014, BuzzFeed raised $50 million from the [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital") firm [Andreessen Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz"), more than doubling previous rounds of funding.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-CNN-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-46) The site was reportedly valued at around $850 million by Andreessen Horowitz.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-CNN-45) BuzzFeed generates its advertising revenue through [native advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising "Native advertising") that matches its editorial content, and does not rely on banner ads.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-insidebuzzfeed-17) BuzzFeed also uses its familiarity with social media to target conventional advertising through other channels, such as Facebook.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-fastcompany-47) In December 2014, growth equity firm [General Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Atlantic "General Atlantic") acquired $50 million in secondary stock of the company.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-48)

In August 2015, [NBCUniversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBCUniversal "NBCUniversal") made a $200 million [equity investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_investment "Equity investment") in BuzzFeed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-49) Along with plans to hire more journalists to build a more prominent "investigative" unit, BuzzFeed planned on hiring journalists around the world and plans to open outposts in India, Germany, Mexico, and Japan.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-50) It planned on hiring staff for its UK bureau, its rapidly-expanding motion picture unit and its food-themed business, Tasty.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-52) NBCUniversal invested an additional $200 million in 2016 after the two companies had collaborated on many projects, namely the [Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Reuters_2016-44) The companies planned to work together to market themselves to advertisers.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Reuters_2016-44) Together, Comcast and its NBCUniversal subsidiary own about a third of BuzzFeed. BuzzFeed has said that it intends to stay independent.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-53)

After laying off 100 employees in 2017, BuzzFeed laid off 200 of its employees in 2019 to help facilitate growth despite raising revenue by 15% from 2017 to 2018.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-axios.com-54)[Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") began funding two BuzzFeed News shows in 2019 for [Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook_Watch "Facebook Watch").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-axios.com-54) Because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), on March 25, 2020, BuzzFeed announced in an internal memo that it would cut employee salaries on a sliding scale of 5% (lowest income bracket) up to 25% (highest income bracket). Peretti said he would not be taking a salary until the end of the pandemic. Many staffers expressed relief at this announcement as there were no layoffs.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-55) On May 13, 2020, the company shut down its divisions in the UK and Australia, furloughing 10 news staff in the UK as well as four in its Australian outpost.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-57)

According to a news from June 24, 2021 on Variety, BuzzFeed, valued at $1.5 billion through a SPAC deal, is to go public and acquire Complex Networks for $300 million.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-59)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-60)

BuzzFeed raised $16.2M in its latest funding round, which was Post IPO round held on Dec 03, 2021.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-61)

In 2025, BuzzFeed had a net loss of $57.3 million, noting that it did not have enough resources to fund its cash obligations for 2026,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-auto-32) stating that "there is substantial doubt about the Company's ability to continue as a going concern."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:4-31)

### Acquisitions and stock listing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Acquisitions and stock listing")]

BuzzFeed's first acquisition was in 2012 when the company purchased Kingfish Labs, a startup founded by [Rob Fishman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Fishman "Rob Fishman"), initially focused on optimizing Facebook ads.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-62)

In October 2014, BuzzFeed announced its next acquisition, Torando Labs, which would become BuzzFeed's first data-engineering team.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-63)

On November 19, 2020, BuzzFeed announced that they would acquire _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ in a stock deal that made [Verizon Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon_Media "Verizon Media") minority shareholder in BuzzFeed.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-66)

In June 2021, BuzzFeed announced its plans to go public via a [special-purpose acquisition company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special-purpose_acquisition_company "Special-purpose acquisition company") (SPAC) and planned to acquire [Complex Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_Networks "Complex Networks").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-67) After initially listing on [Nasdaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq "Nasdaq") at $10 a share, valuing the company at around $1.5 billion, the share price subsequently declined to [under $1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_stock "Penny stock") by 2023, leading to a [delisting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delisting_(stock) "Delisting (stock)") notice by Nasdaq in May 2023, requiring them to raise the share price above $1 within 180 days or risk being removed from the exchange.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-68) Once the deadline for this notice passed in November 2023 with the stock price still below $1, they were given a further 180 days until May 2024.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-69) By January 2024, the stock price of the company had declined 98% since its initial listing, with the entire company now only worth around $37 million, and the company was significantly burdened with debt.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-70) In May 2024, BuzzFeed implemented a 4:1 [reverse stock split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_stock_split "Reverse stock split"), bringing them above the $1 a share threshold.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-71)

In May 2024, activist investor [Vivek Ramaswamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivek_Ramaswamy "Vivek Ramaswamy") acquired a 7.7% stake in BuzzFeed, making him the fourth-largest shareholder,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-72) which he later increased to 8.37%.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:3-73) Ramaswamy said that he thought the company was undervalued,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:0-74) and that he wanted to shift the company's political leanings[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:3-73) such as by hiring right-wing media personalities.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-75) Elizabeth Lopatto, writing in _The Verge_, called his effort futile, as voting power in BuzzFeed is primarily in Class B shares, which have 50 times the voting power of the common Class A shares Ramaswamy had purchased. 90% of Class B shares are held by founder Peretti and close associates, meaning that Ramaswamy has little voting power despite his large shareholding.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-76)

By March 2026 the stock price had fallen under $1 again to around $0.66-0.75 a share, and Nasdaq again threatened to delist the stock.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:5-37)

### Divestitures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Divestitures")]

In February 2024, BuzzFeed announced the sale of Complex to NTWRK, a livestream shopping platform, even as it would retain some popular franchises. At the same time, it reportedly considered selling Tasty, a social media food brand. The moves marked a retreat for the company after its December 2021 public listing done to finance acquisitions and came during a difficult period for media companies. It also announced layoffs.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-78)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-80) In July 2024, the company sold travel-brand Bring Me! to media publisher LOST iN.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-81) In December 2024, BuzzFeed sold [First We Feast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_We_Feast "First We Feast"), which produces the show [Hot Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Ones "Hot Ones"), for $82.5 million to a consortium of investors.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-82) According to Reuters, in early 2024 British media group [The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent") reportedly discussed a multi-year agreement to acquire control of BuzzFeed and HuffPost's operations in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-83)

## Film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Film")]

## Content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Content")]

BuzzFeed produces daily content, in which the work of staff reporters, contributors, syndicated cartoon artists, and its community are featured. Popular formats on the website include lists, videos, and quizzes. The style of such content inspired the parody website [ClickHole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ClickHole "ClickHole").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-LaFrance&Meyer-Atlantic-3)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-slate-ClickHole-91) While BuzzFeed initially was focused exclusively on such viral content, according to _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, "it added more traditional content, building a track record for delivering breaking news and deeply reported articles" in the years up to 2014.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-nytimes.com-92) In that year, BuzzFeed deleted over 4000 early posts, "apparently because, as time passed, they looked stupider and stupider", as observed by _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-93)

BuzzFeed consistently ranked at the top of [NewsWhip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewsWhip "NewsWhip")'s "Facebook Publisher Rankings" from December 2013 to April 2014, until _The Huffington Post_ entered the position.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-94)

### News

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: News")]

Main article: [BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed_News "BuzzFeed News")

BuzzFeed's news division began in December 2011 with the appointment of Ben Smith as editor-in-chief. In 2013, Pulitzer Prize winner [Mark Schoofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Schoofs "Mark Schoofs") of [ProPublica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProPublica "ProPublica") was hired as head of [investigative reporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_reporting "Investigative reporting").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Mullin-Poynter-2017-95) By 2016, BuzzFeed had 20 investigative journalists.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-:1-7) Chief executive Jonah Peretti announced the BuzzFeed News division would close on April 20, 2023.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-97)

### Video

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Video")]

BuzzFeed Video, BuzzFeed Motion Picture's flagship [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-98) produces original content. Its production studio and team are based in Los Angeles. Since hiring [Ze Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ze_Frank "Ze Frank") in 2012, BuzzFeed Video has produced several video series, including "[The Try Guys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Try_Guys "The Try Guys")". They also created _You Do You_ and its spinoff _[Unfortunately Ashly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ash\_Perez "Ash Perez")_. In August 2014, the company announced a new division, BuzzFeed Motion Pictures, which may produce feature-length films.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-nytimes.com-92) As of September 1, 2021, BuzzFeed Video's YouTube channel had garnered more than 17.4 billion views and more than 20.3 million subscribers.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-99) BuzzFeed later announced that YouTube signed on for two feature-length series to be created by BuzzFeed Motion Pictures, entitled _[Broke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broke\_(2017\_TV\_series) "Broke (2017 TV series)")_ and _[Squad Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squad\_Wars "Squad Wars")_.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-100)
