## Notable stories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Notable stories")]

### "The dress"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: \"The dress\"")]

Main article: [The dress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_dress "The dress")

> The most interesting thing to me is that it traveled. It went from New York media circle-jerk Twitter to international. And you could see it in my Twitter notifications because people started having conversations in, like, Spanish and Portuguese and then Japanese and Chinese and Thai and Arabic. It was amazing to watch this move from a local thing to, like, a massive international phenomenon.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-OralHistory-132)

—Cates Holderness

In February 2015, a post resulting in a debate over the color of an item of clothing from BuzzFeed's Tumblr editor Cates Holderness garnered more than 28 million views in one day, setting a record for most concurrent visitors to a BuzzFeed post.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-133) Holderness had shown the picture to other members of the site's [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") team, who immediately began arguing about the dress colors among themselves. After creating a simple poll for users of the site, she left work and took [the subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") back to her [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") home. When she got off the train and checked her telephone, it was overwhelmed by the messages on various sites. "I couldn't open [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") because it kept crashing. I thought somebody had died, maybe. I didn't know what was going on." Later in the evening the page set a new record at BuzzFeed for [concurrent visitors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_(web_analytics) "Session (web analytics)"), which reached 673,000 at its peak.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-OralHistory-132)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-BBCNews1January2016-134)

### Watermelon stunt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Watermelon stunt")]

Main article: [Exploding watermelon stunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploding_watermelon_stunt "Exploding watermelon stunt")

On April 8, 2016, two BuzzFeed interns created a live stream on [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook"), during which rubber bands were wrapped one by one around a [watermelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon "Watermelon") until the pressure [caused it to explode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploding_watermelon_stunt "Exploding watermelon stunt"). _The Daily Dot_ compared it to something from _[America's Funniest Home Videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America's\_Funniest\_Home\_Videos "America's Funniest Home Videos")_ or by the comedian [Gallagher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallagher_(comedian) "Gallagher (comedian)"), and "just as stupid-funny, but with incredible immediacy and zero production costs". The video is seen as part of Facebook's strategy to shift to live video, [Facebook Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook_Live "Facebook Live"), to counter the rise of [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") and [Periscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periscope_(app) "Periscope (app)") among a younger audience.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-dailydot-135)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Criticism")]

### Plagiarism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Plagiarism")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Benny_Johnson_%2812555523704%29.jpg/250px-Benny_Johnson_%2812555523704%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Benny_Johnson_(12555523704).jpg)

[Benny Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Johnson_(journalist) "Benny Johnson (journalist)") was fired from BuzzFeed in July 2014 for plagiarism.

BuzzFeed has been accused of plagiarizing original content from competitors from the online and offline press. In June 2012, [Gawker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawker "Gawker")'s [Adrian Chen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Chen "Adrian Chen") observed that one of BuzzFeed's most popular writers—[Matt Stopera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Stopera "Matt Stopera")—frequently copied and pasted "chunks of text into lists without attribution."[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-gawkplag-136) In March 2013, _[The Atlantic Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic\_Wire "The Atlantic Wire")_ also reported several "listicles" had apparently been copied from [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit") and other websites.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-137) In July 2014, BuzzFeed writer [Benny Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Johnson_(journalist) "Benny Johnson (journalist)") was accused of multiple instances of plagiarism.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-politcoplag-138) Two anonymous Twitter users chronicled Johnson attributing work that was not his own, but "directly lift[ed] from other reporters, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia"), and [Yahoo! Answers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Answers "Yahoo! Answers")", all without credit.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-139) BuzzFeed editor Ben Smith initially defended Johnson, calling him a "deeply original writer".[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-farhi-140) Days later, Smith acknowledged that Johnson had plagiarized the work of others 40 times and announced that Johnson had been fired, apologizing to BuzzFeed readers. "Plagiarism, much less copying unchecked facts from Wikipedia or other sources, is an act of disrespect to the reader", Smith said. "We are deeply embarrassed and sorry to have misled you."[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-farhi-140) In total, 41 instances of plagiarism were found and corrected.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-141) In 2016, claims surfaced of the YouTube channel BuzzFeedVideo stealing ideas and content from other creators.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-142)

BuzzFeed has been the subject of multiple copyright infringement lawsuits, for both using content it had no rights to and encouraging its proliferation without attributing its sources: one for an individual photographer's photograph,[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-143) and another for nine celebrity photographs from a single photography company.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-144)

In June 2020, [BuzzFeed News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed_News "BuzzFeed News") senior reporter [Ryan Broderick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Broderick "Ryan Broderick") was fired after it was revealed he had "plagiarized or misattributed information in at least 11 of his articles."[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-TheWrap_2020-145)

### Reputation as a news site

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Reputation as a news site")]

In October 2014, a [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") survey[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-146) found that in the United States, BuzzFeed was viewed as an unreliable source by the majority of people, regardless of political affiliation.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Zhang_2014-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-148)_[Adweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adweek "Adweek")_ noted that most respondents had not heard of BuzzFeed, and many users do not consider BuzzFeed a news site.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-149) In a subsequent Pew report based on 2014 surveys,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-150) BuzzFeed was among the least trusted sources by [millennials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennials "Millennials").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-151)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-152) A 2016 study by the _[Columbia Journalism Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia\_Journalism\_Review "Columbia Journalism Review")_ found readers less likely to trust a story (originally published in _[Mother Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother\_Jones\_(magazine) "Mother Jones (magazine)")_) that appeared to originate on BuzzFeed than the same article on _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ website.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-153) In a 2017 survey among US readers, BuzzFeed was voted the second least trustworthy source among American readers, with [Occupy Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy_Democrats "Occupy Democrats") being lower-ranked.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-154)

In January 2017, BuzzFeed again faced widespread criticism from many journalists and media officials, along with then-President elect [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), for publishing 35 pages of unverified memos in full, known as the [Steele dossier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steele_dossier "Steele dossier").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-155)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-money.cnn.com-156)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-157)[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-158) In a highly publicized press conference following the publication of the memos, Trump referred to BuzzFeed as a "failing pile of garbage".[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-159) Among the unverified claims in the memos was one that stated Trump's attorney [Michael Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cohen_(lawyer) "Michael Cohen (lawyer)") had met in August 2016 with Russian officials in [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"), [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic"), a claim that Cohen has vehemently denied.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-money.cnn.com-156)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-160)

On January 18, 2019, [Robert Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller "Robert Mueller")'s office disputed a BuzzFeed report stating that Trump instructed [Michael Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cohen_(lawyer) "Michael Cohen (lawyer)") to lie to Congress. A spokesman for Mueller's office characterized the BuzzFeed report as "not accurate".[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-polantz-161)

### Unpaid contributors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Unpaid contributors")]

[Matthew Perpetua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Perpetua "Matthew Perpetua"), BuzzFeed's director of quizzes, published a blog post in January 2019 after being laid off, revealing that many of the site's most popular quizzes were created by unpaid contributors.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Fluxblog_2019-162) Perpetua identified one college student in [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") in particular as "the second-highest traffic driver worldwide."[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_2019-163) The student, Rachel McMahon, said that until she saw Perpetua's blog post, she never knew that her quizzes were so significant for BuzzFeed's traffic. The quizzes made an estimated $3.8 million for the media company.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-164) According to the _[Detroit Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit\_Free\_Press "Detroit Free Press")_, she had never asked BuzzFeed about getting paid and the only material goods she received from them were four $30 [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") gift certificates, a BuzzFeed sweatshirt and T-shirt and several water bottles.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-165)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-166)

### Advertiser influence on editorial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Advertiser influence on editorial")]

In April 2015, BuzzFeed drew scrutiny after [Gawker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawker "Gawker") observed the publication had deleted two posts that criticized advertisers.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-167) One of the posts criticized [Dove soap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_(toiletries) "Dove (toiletries)") (manufactured by [Unilever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unilever "Unilever")), while another criticized [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro").[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-168) Both companies advertise with BuzzFeed. Ben Smith apologized in a memo to staff for his actions: "I blew it. Twice in the past couple of months, I've asked editors—over their better judgment and without any respect to our standards or process—to delete recently published posts from the site. Both involved the same thing: my overreaction to questions we've been wrestling with about the place of personal opinion pieces on our site. I reacted impulsively when I saw the posts and I was wrong to do that. We've reinstated both with a brief note".[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-169) Days later, [Arabelle Sicardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabelle_Sicardi "Arabelle Sicardi"), one of the authors of the deleted posts, resigned.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-170) An internal review by the company found three additional posts deleted for being critical of products or advertisements (by [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"), [Pepsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsi "Pepsi"), and Unilever).[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-171)

In 2016, the [Advertising Standards Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising_Standards_Authority_(United_Kingdom) "Advertising Standards Authority (United Kingdom)") of the United Kingdom ruled that BuzzFeed broke the UK advertising rules for failing to make it clear that an article on "14 Laundry Fails We've All Experienced" that promoted [Dylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylon "Dylon") was an online [advertorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertorial "Advertorial") paid for by the brand.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-172)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-GuardianASA-173) Although the ASA agreed with BuzzFeed's defense that links to the piece from its homepage and search results clearly labelled the article as "sponsored content", this failed to take into account that individuals might link to the story directly, ruling that the labeling "was not sufficient to make clear that the main content of the web page was an advertorial and that editorial content was therefore retained by the advertiser".[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-GuardianASA-173)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-174)

### Hiring practices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Hiring practices")]

In February 2016, [Scaachi Koul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaachi_Koul "Scaachi Koul"), a Senior Writer for BuzzFeed Canada, tweeted a request for pitches stating that BuzzFeed was "...looking for mostly non-white non-men" followed by "If you are a white man upset that we are looking mostly for non-white non-men I don't care about you go write for Maclean's." When confronted, she followed with the tweet "White men are still permitted to pitch, I will read it, I will consider it. I'm just less interested because, ugh, men." In response to the tweets that were deemed [racist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism") and [sexist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexism "Sexism"), Koul began receiving a barrage of hate comments and threats of violence.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-175)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-176) Sarmishta Subramanian, a former colleague of Koul's, writing for _[Maclean's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maclean's "Maclean's")_, condemned the reaction to the tweets, and stated that Koul's request for diversity was appropriate. Subramanian said that her provocative approach raised concerns of [tokenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokenism "Tokenism") that might hamper BuzzFeed's stated goals.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-177) In January 2019, BuzzFeed announced that it would cut its workforce by 15%.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-178) In July 2019 BuzzFeed announced that it would voluntarily recognize an employee union.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-179)

### Ideology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Ideology")]

BuzzFeed states in its editorial guide that "we firmly believe that for a number of issues, including civil rights, women's rights, anti-racism, and LGBT equality, there are not two sides."[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-180)_[The Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Week "The Week")_'s correspondent Ryan Cooper and [American Enterprise Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute "American Enterprise Institute")'s senior fellow [Timothy P. Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_P._Carney "Timothy P. Carney") at the _[Washington Examiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Examiner "Washington Examiner")_ raised questions about whether BuzzFeed undermines its credibility by taking sides on political issues.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-181)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-182) In June 2015, BuzzFeed and websites like the _Huffington Post_ and [Mashable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashable "Mashable") temporarily changed the theme of their social media avatars to rainbow colors to celebrate same-sex marriage being ruled constitutional in the United States.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-183)

In June 2016, the left-leaning media watchdog [Fairness and Accuracy in Reporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairness_and_Accuracy_in_Reporting "Fairness and Accuracy in Reporting") found that in 100 BuzzFeed stories about [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), 65 were positive, 34 were neutral, and one was critical. The report called BuzzFeed's coverage of Obama "creepy" and "almost uniformly uncritical and often sycophantic."[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-184) BuzzFeed has partnered with Obama on a [get-out-the-vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_out_the_vote "Get out the vote") campaign.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-185) During the same month, BuzzFeed cancelled an advertising agreement with the [Republican National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee "Republican National Committee") over what BuzzFeed founder Jonah Peretti called "offensive remarks" made by [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"). Peretti said: "We certainly don't like to turn away revenue that funds all the important work we do across the company. However, in some cases we must make business exceptions: we don't run cigarette ads because they are hazardous to our health, and we won't accept Trump ads for the exact same reason."[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-186)

In January 2017, BuzzFeed released what became known as the "[Steele dossier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steele_dossier "Steele dossier")", an uncorroborated private intelligence report that alleges several salacious accusations of Trump. [Margaret Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Sullivan_(journalist) "Margaret Sullivan (journalist)") at _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ wrote of the release: "It's a bad idea, and always has been, to publish unverified smears."[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-187) David Graham at _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ called it "an abdication of the basic responsibility of journalism."[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-188)[NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC")'s [Chuck Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Todd "Chuck Todd") called the release of the document "[fake news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_news "Fake news")".[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-189) Ben Smith defended the decision to release the document from accusations that it was done out of partisanship, arguing that the dossier is of "obvious central public importance."[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-190)

## Awards and recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BuzzFeed&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Awards and recognition")]

In 2017, BuzzFeed won [Webby Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webby_Awards "Webby Awards") for Best News App and Best Interview/Talk Show (for _[Another Round](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another\_Round\_(podcast) "Another Round (podcast)")_),[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-191) and president Greg Coleman was named Publishing Executive of the Year by _[Digiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digiday "Digiday")_.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-192)

In 2018, staff of BuzzFeed news was a finalist for a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") in their international reporting category for their article that "proved that operatives with apparent ties to [Vladimir Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin") have engaged in a targeted killing campaign against his perceived enemies on British and American soil".[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-193) BuzzFeed later won a Pulitzer Prize in 2021 in the international reporting category for an investigative series about the [Xinjiang internment camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps "Xinjiang internment camps").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed#cite_note-Robertson-9)

# About VICE Digital Publishing

Coming to you from around the world, VICE Digital’s team strives to capture the people at the heart of stories, and focus on the ideas, issues, and context that other outlets miss.

You can find our award-winning work **online**; [**on YouTube**](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCn8zNIfYAQNdrFRrr8oibKw); [**in a print magazine**](https://www.vice.com/en/article/vice-magazine-is-coming-back/); [**in newsletters**](https://newsletter.vice.com/subscribe), and [**on Facebook**](https://www.facebook.com/VICE/), [**Twitter**](https://twitter.com/VICE), [**Snapchat**](https://www.snapchat.com/discover/Vice/0467327245) and [**Instagram**](https://www.instagram.com/vice/).

**How To Reach Us**

If you’re interested in pitching us a story idea, keep reading.

If you’d like to license some of our content, please email licensing@savage.ventures.

For press inquiries, contact us via press@vice.com.

If you’d like to advertise with us, please email sales@vice.com.

VICE.com is owned and operated by VICE Digital Publishing, LLC a [Savage Ventures company](https://www.savage.ventures/).

Savage Ventures address:1402 3rd Ave N Nashville, TN 37208.

**How To Pitch Us**

At VICE, the story has always been the star. The best pitches are succinct and focused. They have a firm grasp on why the story is interesting and original, what makes it a natural fit for VICE, and the reporting that will take it to the next level. When possible, point to specific sources you want to interview and note if access could be an issue. Lastly, tell us why you’re the right person to tell this story. Do you have a foothold in the right communities? What knowledge or expertise do you bring?

Most editors want to work on shaping the story with you, so it’s better not to send completed drafts. Instead, please send a succinct pitch via email to [pitches@savage.ventures](mailto:pitches@savage.ventures).

# About VICE Digital Publishing

Coming to you from around the world, VICE Digital’s team strives to capture the people at the heart of stories, and focus on the ideas, issues, and context that other outlets miss.

You can find our award-winning work **online**; [**on YouTube**](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCn8zNIfYAQNdrFRrr8oibKw); [**in a print magazine**](https://www.vice.com/en/article/vice-magazine-is-coming-back/); [**in newsletters**](https://newsletter.vice.com/subscribe), and [**on Facebook**](https://www.facebook.com/VICE/), [**Twitter**](https://twitter.com/VICE), [**Snapchat**](https://www.snapchat.com/discover/Vice/0467327245) and [**Instagram**](https://www.instagram.com/vice/).

**Vice Media Group LLC** is a Canadian-American [digital media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media "Digital media") and [broadcasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcasting "Broadcasting") company. As of April 2024,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit) Vice Media encompasses four main business areas: Vice Studios Group (film and TV production); [Vice TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_TV "Vice TV") (a joint venture with [A&E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks"), also known as [Viceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceland "Viceland")); Virtue (an agency offering creative services); and [Vice Digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine)#Website "Vice (magazine)") (digital content).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Lodderhose-2) It was cited as the largest independent youth media company in the world, with 35 offices.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-nine2021-9)

The original _[Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)")_ magazine was founded and based in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), and co-founded by Suroosh Alvi,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:4-10)[Shane Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist) "Shane Smith (journalist)"), and [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-auto1-11) Developed from the magazine, Vice Media expanded primarily into youth and young adult-focused digital media. This included online content [verticals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_marketing "Vertical marketing") and related [web series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_series "Web series"), a [news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News "News") division, a film production studio, and a [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label"), among other properties. Vice re-located to New York City in 2001.

[Vice News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News "Vice News") was known for broadcasting news programs on [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO"); including the [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award "Emmy Award")-winning[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-12) weekly [self-titled documentary series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(TV_series) "Vice (TV series)"), which premiered in April 2013, and features segments on global issues hosted by co-founders Smith and Alvi, and a rotating cast of correspondents.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICESeason5HBO-14) A spin-off, _[Vice News Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_News\_Tonight "Vice News Tonight")_, premiered 10 October 2016 and showcased a nightly roundup of global news, technology, [the environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment"), economics, and pop culture while eschewing traditional news anchors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICENewsTonightPostponesLauch-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICENewscastsnet-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:0-17)

On 10 June 2019, HBO announced _Vice News Tonight'_ s cancellation, in addition to ending relations with Vice Media, after a seven-year partnership.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-18) In August 2019, it was reported that the company was laying off staff as part of a shift towards news that would involve merging Viceland and Vice News.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Mullin-19) In April 2023, it was announced that Vice Media was restructuring and downsizing its news division.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:6-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:7-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:8-22) A month later, once valued at $5.7 billion, Vice filed for [Chapter 11 bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11,_Title_11,_United_States_Code "Chapter 11, Title 11, United States Code")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-c11-23) and agreed to be acquired by a consortium led by [Fortress Investment Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_Investment_Group "Fortress Investment Group") for $350 million in June.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:5-24)

In February of 2024, Vice's former CEO Bruce Dixon announced additional layoffs and that [Vice.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine)#Website "Vice (magazine)") would cease publishing content.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:9-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:10-26) In July 2025, Vice published new content.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-27) Vice has since partnered with other media companies, such as Savage Ventures, to distribute its content.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-savage-28)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding and early years (1994–2005)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding and early years (1994–2005)")]

_Voice_ (later _Voices of Montreal_) was founded by Alix Laurent of Interimages Communications in October 1994, with Suroosh Alvi as editor and [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes") as assistant editor, with Shane Smith joining the magazine's staff later. It initially focused on [drug culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_culture "Drug culture"), [skateboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skateboarding "Skateboarding"), [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art "Art"), [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music"), and [trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trends "Trends").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Voice_of_Montreal_Magazine_V01_N01-29)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:4-10)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Bazilian2014-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Rob-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-32) The magazine focused on Montreal's alternative cultural scene, to compete with the already established _[Montreal Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal\_Mirror "Montreal Mirror")_. Alvi, McInnes and Smith bought out the publisher and changed the magazine's name to _Vice_ in 1996.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-33)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Bazilian2014-30)

As the magazine became more successful, the company received an investment of $4 million by Canadian investor Richard Szalwinski and _Vice_ relocated to New York City in 1999. In 2001, the co-founders bought _Vice_ back and moved to new offices in [Williamsburg, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williamsburg,_Brooklyn "Williamsburg, Brooklyn").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:2-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-35)

### Digital expansion (2006–2011)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Digital expansion (2006–2011)")]

In 2006, on the advice of creative director [Spike Jonze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jonze "Spike Jonze"), Vice began expanding into digital video, launching new video service [VBS.tv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VBS.tv "VBS.tv") as a joint venture with [MTV Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_Media_Networks "Viacom Media Networks").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-wired-tanz-36)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Rob-31) VBS gained a fan base with shows like _The Vice Guide To Travel_, _Epicly Later'd_, _Toxic_ and _Hamilton's Pharmacopeia_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-37)

In 2007, Vice Media began expanding its digital video operation, launching new channels, such as _Motherboard_ (tech), _Noisey_ (music), and _The Creators Project,_ an arts/technology site founded in partnership with [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel"). Vice Media would later launch sites around [electronic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") culture (_Thump_), global news (_Vice News_), food (_Munchies_) and sports (_Vice Sports_). Additionally, Vice Media launched Virtue Worldwide, a creative services agency, to expand their capabilities for work around their platforms.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-38) During this time, Santiago Stelley was the director of content of VBS.tv (2006–2010) and creative director of Vice Media (2010–2012).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-39)

In January 2008, co-founder Gavin McInnes left Vice Media due to "creative differences" with the company,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-auto1-11) and founded the website _streetcarnage.com_. He later co-founded _Rooster_, an advertising agency, and became a far-right activist, founding the [Proud Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proud_Boys "Proud Boys").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-40)

According to _[Columbia Journalism Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia\_Journalism\_Review "Columbia Journalism Review")_, Vice has altered shots during the editing process in pursuit of more entertaining or impressive scenes. In a 2011 documentary on Libya, a voiceover from the reporter claims that he had gone to the frontlines amidst an offensive, while in contrast a source claims the reporter did not make the trip, with only a cameraman going there.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:3-41)

### Further expansion (2012–2017)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Further expansion (2012–2017)")]

In 2012, Vice Media continued to expand its coverage focused around news and current events.

With the end of VBS.tv, _Vice_ began releasing films like _UK's Scariest Debt Collector_, _Swansea Love Story, World's Scariest Drug_ and _Inside the Superhuman World of the Iceman_ through their main website and [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel, as well as new series like _Slutever_, _Fringes_, _Love Industry_ and _High Society_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-42)

In mid-August 2013, [Rupert Murdoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Murdoch "Rupert Murdoch")'s [21st Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Century_Fox "21st Century Fox") invested US$70 million in Vice Media, resulting in a 5% stake. Following the announcement, Smith explained: "We have set ourselves up to build a global platform but we have maintained control."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-43) In 2013, Vice Media premiered a new 30-minute news program for [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") titled [_Vice_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(TV_series) "Vice (TV series)"), executive produced by [Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher "Bill Maher"). In 2014, the second season of the show won a [Creative Arts Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Arts_Emmy_Award "Creative Arts Emmy Award") for Outstanding Informational Series or Special in the [66th Primetime Creative Arts Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/66th_Primetime_Creative_Arts_Emmy_Awards "66th Primetime Creative Arts Emmy Awards").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-44) In 2014, Vice Media launched its news channel, [Vice News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News "Vice News"), which almost immediately gained global attention for its coverage of protests and conflict in [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euromaidan "Euromaidan") and [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuelan_protests_(2014%E2%80%93present) "Venezuelan protests (2014–present)"). As of October 2014, the editor of BBC Radio 1's _Newsbeat_ claimed the BBC was "playing catch-up" to Vice News.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-45)

Vice Media has routinely advocated for their "immersionist" brand of journalism in the pursuit of more authentic and interesting stories. Their founders and editors have regularly garnered controversy from the likes of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_'[David Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carr_(journalist) "David Carr (journalist)"), who bristled in an exchange with Shane Smith in the 2011 documentary _[Page One: Inside the New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page\_One:\_Inside\_the\_New\_York\_Times "Page One: Inside the New York Times")._ In a 2014 _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ column, Carr said that _Vice_ had since grown into a strong news entity. In August 2014, Carr published a _New York Times_ column further reversing his earlier criticism of Vice, saying: "Being the crusty old-media scold felt good at the time, but recent events suggest that Vice is deadly serious about doing real news that people, yes, even young people, will actually watch."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-46)

On 2 July 2014, Vice Media announced that it would be relocating into a warehouse space in Williamsburg that had been occupied by the independent arts spaces and concert venues [285 Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/285_KENT "285 KENT"), [Death by Audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_By_Audio "Death By Audio") and [Glasslands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasslands_Gallery "Glasslands Gallery"), among others. Vice and the building property owners facilitated the clearance of the building and the displacement of the existing creative tenants.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-47) Vice spent US$20 million to renovate the 60,000-square-foot (5,600 m 2) building as part of an eight-year lease,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-48) facilitating the establishment of new production facilities with full broadcast capabilities, and received an offer of US$6.5 million in [tax credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_credit "Tax credit") from New York state's Empire State Development.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-49) In August 2014, [A&E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks"), a television group jointly owned by [The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") and [Hearst Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearst_Communications "Hearst Communications"), made a US$250-million investment in Vice Media for an ownership stake of 10%.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Bond2014-50) In November and December 2015, Disney made two additional individual investments of US$200 million totalling $400 million.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-DisneyInvestsinVICE-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-52)

On 26 March 2015, HBO announced it would renew its contract to broadcast the weekly _Vice_ documentary series for four years, while expanding the annual broadcast schedule from 14 to nearly 30 episodes.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-53) The network also announced Vice would be launching a nightly news program. The show, entitled _Vice News Tonight_, premiered on 10 October 2016 and was planned to run 48 weeks each year, featuring pre-edited video and graphics segments covering global news, technology, the environment, economics and pop culture, while eschewing the use of live TV anchors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICENewsTonightPostponesLauch-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICENewscastsnet-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:0-17)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-54) In November 2015, Vice and A&E Networks announced [Viceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceland "Viceland"), a then-upcoming cable network that would feature Vice-produced content.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-thr-viceland-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-nyt-viceland-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-deadline-vicerebrand-57)

On 14 March 2017, Vice announced an expanded original programming deal with [Snap Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_Inc. "Snap Inc."). The new deal built on Vice's previous deal to serve as a 2015 global launch partner on the [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") Discover platform. The first program planned under the new deal was _Hungry Hearts with [Action Bronson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action\_Bronson "Action Bronson")_, starring the titular rapper.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-58) That same month, Vice announced a wide range of content deals which would make its programming available in more than 80 territories by the end of 2017.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:1-59)

In June 2017, Vice secured a $450 million investment from private-equity firm [TPG Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TPG_Capital "TPG Capital") to increase spending on scripted programming and ongoing international expansion. As a result of the deal, Vice Media was valued at $5.7 billion.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-60) In September 2018, Disney wrote down its investment in Vice by $157 million. Disney acquired Fox's stake in Vice when [its acquisition of 21st Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquisition_of_21st_Century_Fox_by_Disney "Acquisition of 21st Century Fox by Disney") completed in March 2019.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-61)

On 23 December 2017, _The New York Times_ reported that there had been four settlements involving allegations of [sexual harassment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_harassment "Sexual harassment") or [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation") against Vice employees. In addition, over 20 other women stated that they had experienced or witnessed [sexual misconduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_misconduct "Sexual misconduct"), including unwanted kisses, groping, lewd remarks and propositions for sex at the company. In a statement provided to _The New York Times_, Vice co-founders Shane Smith and Suroosh Alvi said, "from the top down, we have failed as a company to create a safe and inclusive workplace where everyone, especially women, can feel respected and thrive."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-64)

In January 2018, Vice's COO/CFO Sarah Broderick sent a memo to staff on 2 January 2018 announcing President Creighton had volunteered to go on temporary leave whilst a new investigation into a $135,000 settlement from a case the company paid in 2016 to a former employee who alleged she was fired after turning him down, and the suspension of Mike Germano, who had served as chief digital officer. Germano founded Carrot Creative, which was acquired by Vice in 2013; he was accused of pulling a former colleague onto his lap at a company party, as well as telling his former strategist Amanda Rue he originally did not want to hire her "because he wanted to have sex with her."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-65) Vice has also been criticized by current and former employees for featuring work by [Terry Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Richardson "Terry Richardson"), a photographer facing accusations of [sexual abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_abuse "Sexual abuse") by multiple models.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:3-41) In another documentary, a former female employee covering a story about sex workers in a developing country said Vice attempted to "sensationalize and exploit" the women depicted. In one occasion, producers requested her to go undercover as a prostitute, which she refused. She also remarks being oriented to swear more while on camera.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:3-41)

### Decline (2018–2022)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Decline (2018–2022)")]

In March 2018, Vice Media co-founder [Shane Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist) "Shane Smith (journalist)") announced he would no longer continue as CEO and would take on the new title of Executive Chairman. Former [A+E Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&E_Networks "A&E Networks") CEO [Nancy Dubuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Dubuc "Nancy Dubuc") succeeded Smith as CEO.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-66) "Smith will now be focused on creating content and strategic deals and partnerships to help grow the company."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-67) On 20 August 2018, Vice's _Munchies_ and Fremantle Media signed a deal with Triple Five Group to gain control of the food hall at American Dream Meadowlands. The food hall was expected to open in April 2019.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-69) In November 2018, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that Vice Media was looking to trim its workforce by 10–15%, relying on attrition rather than layoffs.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-70) The same month, CEO Nancy Dubuc told an audience at _The New York Times_ Dealbook conference that Vice would return to profitability the following year.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-73) In March 2019, it was reported that Vice Media was looking to raise another $200 million in funding.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-75)

On 1 May 2019, Vice consolidated many of its web channels back into one central platform turning them into feature sections. The move included independent _Munchies_, _Noisey_, _Motherboard_, _Broadly_, _Free_, _Amuse_, _Tonic_, _Waypoint_, and _Vice Sports_. Vice also ended its block on the ad industry's keyword blacklist of 25 terms.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Spangler_Spangler_2019-76) On 3 May 2019, Vice Media announced that it raised $250 million in debt from [George Soros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Soros "George Soros") and other investors.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-77) In October, Vice Media announced that it was acquiring _[Refinery29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refinery29 "Refinery29")_.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Spangler2019-78) The deal, worth a reported $400 million,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-79) valued the combined company at $4 billion.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Spangler2019-78)

In May 2020, Vice Media announced they were laying off more than 150 staff due to financial difficulties.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-81) In June 2020, Vice Media launched an investigation into allegations of subsidiary Refinery29's [toxic work environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxic_workplace "Toxic workplace").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-82)

In March 2020, Vice Media organized the Azimuth Music Festival in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), less than two years after Vice paused all work in Saudi Arabia following the [assassination of Jamal Khashoggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Jamal_Khashoggi "Assassination of Jamal Khashoggi"). Vice's brand was not used on marketing material, and contractors had to sign [non-disclosure agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-disclosure_agreement "Non-disclosure agreement") regarding Vice's involvement. Vice opened a commercial and creative office in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") in 2022.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-guardian-20220201-83) On 2 October 2020, Vice Media Group appointed Nadja Bellan-White as the global CMO, to be in charge of worldwide branding, communications and promotions. It was also announced that Meera Pattni had been promoted to VP Communications, directly reporting to Bellan-White.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-84)

In April 2021, Van Scott, former ABC News communications executive, joined Vice as VP Corporate Communications to lead communications in the US. Scott would report to Laura Misselbrook, Global SVP Communications, based in London.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-85)

In April 2021, Vice Media was criticized by [Cambodians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_people "Khmer people") after publishing colorized images of the victims of the [Khmer Rouge Genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Rouge_Genocide "Khmer Rouge Genocide"), some of which had smiles [photoshopped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoshop_(verb) "Photoshop (verb)") onto their faces. Vice later admitted to the images being photoshopped and said that "We regret the error and will investigate how this failure of the editorial process occurred."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-87)

In March 2021, it was claimed that "VICE Media Group is the world's largest independent youth media company", with offices in 35 cities across the world. Its five key businesses were listed as: Vice.com (digital content); Vice Studios (film and TV production); Vice TV; Vice News; and Virtue (an agency offering creative services).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-nine2021-9) In September 2021, it was reported that Vice raised another investment round following cancelled plans to go public via [special purpose acquisition company (SPAC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special-purpose_acquisition_company "Special-purpose acquisition company").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-88)

In 2022, Vice Media experienced severe financial and operational headwinds. Failing to meet its $700 million revenue target, they fell at $100 million, but they ended up with $600 million.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-89)Despite the shortfall and stalled sale talks with [Antenna Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antenna_Group "Antenna Group"), Vice's news division ended up earning 10 [Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") for its journalism.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-91)

### Bankruptcy and sale (2023–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Bankruptcy and sale (2023–present)")]

In January 2023, Vice began exploring the possibility of selling itself.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-92) On 24 February 2023, Dubuc left as CEO as the company faced problems with turning an annual profit and finding a buyer.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-93) Bruce Dixon and Hozefa Lokhandwala were appointed co-CEOs on 27 February, a few days after Dubuc's departure.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-94) It was announced in April 2023 that Vice Media was restructuring and downsizing its Vice News division due to budget problems. This action included the cancellation of _Vice News Tonight_ and other programs and the layoffs of dozens of employees.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:6-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:7-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:8-22)

On 1 May 2023, _The New York Times_ reported that Vice was preparing to file for [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-95) According to _[Deadline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadline\_Hollywood "Deadline Hollywood")_, Vice's primary debt-holder, [Fortress Investment Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_Investment_Group "Fortress Investment Group"), would likely take control of Vice Media as a result of any [Chapter 11 bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy "Chapter 11 bankruptcy") filing.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-96)

Two weeks later, on 15 May, Vice Media formally filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy as part of a possible sale to a consortium of lenders including [Fortress Investment Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_Investment_Group "Fortress Investment Group"), which would, alongside Soros Fund Management and Monroe Capital, invest $225 million as a credit bid for nearly all of its assets.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-c11-23)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-97) The following month, Vice accepted the consortium's increased offer of $350 million prior to the bankruptcy auction.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-98) The company drew criticism for generous executive compensation packages while employees dealt with layoffs and unpaid company bills.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-99) The sale was closed in August 2023.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-100) Lokhandwala resigned as co-CEO in December, leaving Bruce Dixon as sole CEO.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-White-101)

On 22 February 2024, CEO Bruce Dixon announced "several hundred" additional layoffs as part of a company restructuring.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:9-25) Dixon also announced that the Vice.com website would no longer publish content, instead partnering with other media companies to distribute its content, and that the company was discussing the sale of _Refinery29_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:9-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:10-26)

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ highlighted that "over the past half-decade, Vice has had near annual layoffs and mounting losses, and has filed for bankruptcy, making it the poster child for the battered digital-media industry" and that while "some observers hoped its new owners [...] would reinvest" in the company, Fortress Investment Group had instead "decided to make sweeping cuts".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-102) Chris Thompson of _[Defector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defector\_Media "Defector Media")_ commented that "admirers of Vice's journalism—Vice News and Motherboard, both of which were largely kerploded during Vice's bankruptcy, had made themselves essential with years of excellent reporting—have long daydreamed about a future where its owners and executives stopped trying to turn it into a leprechaun's pot of gold and just allowed it to be a good website. [...] Instead of protecting it as responsible stewards, they treated it more or less the way Paul Cicero treated the Bamboo Lounge in _[Goodfellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodfellas "Goodfellas")_, fattening themselves at its expense until there was nothing left to rob, and then burning it to the ground".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-103)

In April 2024, Vice Media sold _Refinery29_ to _[Essence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essence\_(magazine) "Essence (magazine)")_ magazine owner Sundial Media Group.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:11-104) Later that month, Vice Media announced it had restructured its global production business, now called Vice Studios Group, into five units: Pulse Films, UnTypical (formerly Vice Studios), Vice Studios LatAm, Vice Studios Canada and a news documentary unit. Vice Studios Group will be led by Jamie Hall and Danny Gabai as co-presidents.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Lodderhose-2) In May, Vice Media announced it will create a [joint venture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_venture "Joint venture") with Savage Venture to relaunch its websites, such as Vice.com, _Munchies_, _Motherboard_, and _Noisey_.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-savage-28) In September, Vice Media relaunched its print magazine which had been on hiatus since 2019. Issues will be released quarterly. The company has a goal of reaching 20,000 subscribers within a year.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:12-105)

In June 2025, Vice Media appointed former [NBCUniversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBCUniversal "NBCUniversal") and [Dick Clark Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Clark_Productions "Dick Clark Productions") executive Adam Stotsky as Chief Executive Officer, succeeding Bruce Dixon. The company stated that Stotsky would lead its next phase of growth, focusing on expanding Vice Studios, Vice Sports, Vice Commercials, Vice News, and the advertising agency Virtue.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-107)

As of 2026, Vice continues to its digital and publishing revival, highlighting by the continued return of [the magazine of same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)") with themed editions such as the Spring 2026 "The Not The Photo Issue" and the Summer 2026 "The Self-Destruction Issue".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-109) Following major restructuring and ownership shifts in prior years, the brand was focused heavily on curated quarterly print issues. Vice Media operates as a leaner, more restructured brand focusing on a quarterly print magazine revival, digital niche publishing and expanded sports programming on [VICE TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VICE_TV "VICE TV") including a collaboration with the [Professional Fighters League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Fighters_League "Professional Fighters League") with regional leagues for [MENA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MENA "MENA") and Africa following the company's prior finical resurrecting.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-110)

### Magazine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Magazine")]

Main article: [Vice (magazine)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(magazine) "Vice (magazine)")

Vice began as a counterculture print magazine founded in 1996 in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"), Canada, when Suroosh Alvi, [Gavin McInnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McInnes "Gavin McInnes") and [Shane Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Smith_(journalist) "Shane Smith (journalist)") bought its predecessor, Voice of Montreal.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:2-34)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Voice_of_Montreal_Magazine_V01_N01-29)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:4-10)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-111)

As of April 2017, the magazine's editor-in-chief was Ellis Jones.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-113) The magazine switched to a quarterly publication schedule in 2018, though issues still generally explored a single theme.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-114) The publication was put on hiatus in 2019 and relaunched five years later.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:12-105)_Vice_ magazine includes the work of journalists, columnists, fiction writers, graphic artists and cartoonists, and photographers.

### Vice News

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Vice News")]

Main articles: [Vice News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News "Vice News"), [Vice News Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_News_Tonight "Vice News Tonight"), and [Vice (TV series)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_(TV_series) "Vice (TV series)")

Vice News was Vice's current affairs brand. It consisted of ViceNews.com, and two [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") programs; the weekly documentary series _[Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_(TV\_series) "Vice (TV series)")_, and the nightly news series _[Vice News Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_News\_Tonight "Vice News Tonight")_. Vice News focuses on coverage of events that may not be as well covered by other news sources. On 24 May 2016, Vice Media promoted [Josh Tyrangiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Tyrangiel "Josh Tyrangiel") to oversee a unified Vice News division consisting of _Vice News_, the weekly HBO _Vice_ show, and the daily _Vice News Tonight_.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-115)

Vice News creates content daily, distributing written articles and video on its website and [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-116) In 2015, the channel won two [Peabody Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Awards "Peabody Awards") for its video series _The Islamic State_ and _Last Chance High_.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-117)

In 2013, [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") aired the first 10-episode season of a half-hour [newsmagazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_broadcasting "News broadcasting") known as _[Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_(TV\_series) "Vice (TV series)")_, with [Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher "Bill Maher") as executive producer. The initial season saw international coverage for the season one finale that had Vice play an exhibition basketball game in [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") with [Dennis Rodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Rodman "Dennis Rodman") and the [Harlem Globetrotters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Globetrotters "Harlem Globetrotters"). The show was renewed for a second season, which aired in 2014 and won an Emmy award for Outstanding Informational Series or Special.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-118) The show was picked up for two more 14-episode seasons by HBO in May 2014, which aired in 2015 and 2016. The program is currently in its fifth season, which was expanded to a total of 30 episodes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-VICESeason5HBO-14)

In October 2016, a second Vice News program, a nightly news program called _[Vice News Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_News\_Tonight "Vice News Tonight")_, premiered. The program is slated to run 48 weeks each year, featuring pre-edited video and graphics segments covering global news, technology, the environment, economics and pop culture, while eschewing the use of live TV anchors.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-119)

Following the violent protests by [white supremacists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy "White supremacy"), [white nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_nationalism "White nationalism") and other groups at the [Unite the Right rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unite_the_Right_rally "Unite the Right rally") in [Charlottesville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia "Charlottesville, Virginia"), _Vice News Tonight_ broke from its normal newsmagazine format to devote an entire episode to a documentary film on the events. The episode aired the same weekend as the rally, 14 August 2017. _Charlottesville: Race and Terror_ garnered critical praise, with _[Esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire\_(magazine) "Esquire (magazine)")_ urging readers to "watch it and share it".[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-120) In addition to featuring the video on its subscription streaming channels, HBO agreed to post the entire video on YouTube. Within two weeks, it had more than 44 million views between HBO and online platforms and received many positive reviews.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-125) The episode received a Peabody Award for public service journalism in April 2018.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-127)

On April 27, 2023, it was first announced that Vice Media was restructuring and downsizing its news division due to budget problems. This action included the cancellation of _Vice News Tonight_ and other programs and the layoffs of dozens of employees. In a [tweet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") made by the Vice Union, they criticized the company for repeated layoffs and expressed disappointment over the loss of entire teams. They described the layoffs as part of a pattern where Vice has let go of many who have significantly contributed to the company's success. The Union also condemned the manner of the layoff announcements, which were made via a livestream without opportunity for dialogue and where the executives scarcely acknowledged the ongoing layoffs. The Vice Union has affirmed its support for the affected employees, implying a divergence from the company's past identity as a respected media organization.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:6-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:7-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-:8-22)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-128)

### Virtue Worldwide

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_Media&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Virtue Worldwide")]

On 26 January 2017, Vice announced the consolidation of its in-house agency Virtue with Carrot Creative, a digital and mobile agency Vice acquired in 2013, Pulse Films, a production company Vice acquired in 2016 into the new Virtue Worldwide.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-152)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-153) Based in Brooklyn, New York, the combined 450-person global consultancy provides the services of a full agency network and multi-platform content creation studio. Virtue Worldwide will be led by CEO Lars Hemming Jorgensen.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-Shields2017-3)

Relying on these in-house and acquired agencies, apart from its editorial operations, Vice works with advertisers to create global ad campaigns tailored to the company's younger audience.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-154)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-155) The ads generate revenue from the production of the ad and placement within a given media property.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-156) Vice maintains the separation between the production of branded and hard news content, while some critics contend that their operation "blurs the line between editorial and sponsorship".[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-157) This practice is sometimes referred to as "[native advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising "Native advertising")", due to how ads are often mingled with regular content.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-158) Co-founder Alvi has also said that Vice has had "franchises that were underwritten by sponsors – that's our goal, to get a lot of our news franchises and stories and reports sponsored by advertisers. It's kind of the way news used to be in the fifties: 'Brought to you by Gillette' or whatever it was. We love that model."[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-159)

Some of the brands that Vice has worked with are [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google"), [Unilever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unilever "Unilever"), [Bank of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America"), [Samsung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung "Samsung"), [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota"), [Levi Strauss & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_Strauss_&_Co. "Levi Strauss & Co.") and [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel").[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-160) However, some advertisers have been controversial; Edition Worldwide, a subsidiary of Vice UK, was called "highly irresponsible" by the Campaign for Tobacco Free Kids and other anti-smoking groups for their work producing content for tobacco giant [Philip Morris International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Morris_International "Philip Morris International"). This was seen as unethical by anti-tobacco groups due to the young audience which Vice News usually attracts.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-162) In March 2019, Vice accepted £5M from Philip Morris to promote e-cigarettes to young people.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media#cite_note-163)
